The Board of Directors of the African Development Bank Group has approved a €100 million loan to Gotion Power Morocco to finance the development of an integrated cathode-to-cell lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery gigafactory in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone.

The Bank also plans to mobilise up to an additional €141 million from financial partners to support the implementation of this strategic project, acting as Mandated Lead Arranger under the New African Financial Architecture for Development (NAFAD).

Led by Gotion High-Tech, a top-tier global battery manufacturer headquartered in Hefei, China and listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, the project will establish the first integrated battery manufacturing plant in Africa and the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, producing 10 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery cells and packs for electric vehicles in Phase 1, with plans to expand capacity to 100 GWh. This investment strengthens Morocco’s ambition to become a leading hub for global electric mobility and for green technology value chains.

“Battery storage is the missing link in Africa’s clean energy transition. A facility of this scale, powered primarily by renewable energy, strengthens the foundations for the large-scale integration of solar and wind power, which our grids increasingly depend on. This is exactly the kind of project that will deliver reliable, low-carbon energy while creating green industrial jobs and building the resilient value chains Africa needs to sustain its energy transition,” Kevin Kariuki, the Bank Group’s Vice President for Power, Energy, Climate and Green Growth, said.

“This gigafactory will be a major catalyst for strengthening Morocco’s industrial competitiveness and for accelerating its emergence as Africa’s manufacturing hub for sustainable mobility industries,” noted Achraf Tarsim, the African Development Bank Group’s Country Manager for Morocco. “It will help foster an African industrial ecosystem for batteries and electric vehicles while promoting the local beneficiation of critical minerals essential to the energy transition.”

Beyond its transformative impact on Morocco’s industrial sector, the project is expected to create more than 600 direct jobs in its first phase and achieve a local industrial integration rate of 70%, thereby supporting skills development and the growth of local industrial ecosystems.

The project aligns with the African Development Bank Group’s Four Cardinal Points strategic vision by promoting resilient infrastructure, accelerating industrialisation, adding value to Africa’s natural resources, and strengthening regional integration. It is also expected to strengthen the continent’s position in global clean energy and electric mobility value chains.

By advancing electric mobility and energy storage solutions, the project will help accelerate Africa’s transition to a low-carbon economy and facilitate greater deployment of renewable energy.

text:
Mumbai: L&T announces the successful conclusion of the Framework Cooperation Agreement (FCA) for 2 GW offshore wind programme with TenneT.

L&T, in consortium with Hitachi Energy, entered into FCA covering in principle six projects and future opportunities under TenneT’s ambitious 2-GW HVDC programme. The framework is designed to support large-scale integration of offshore renewable energy and accelerate Europe's transition towards a sustainable and decarbonised clean energy future.

As part of the programme, the consortium will continue the execution of two ongoing projects – IJmuiden Ver Alpha and Nederwiek 1 – in the Netherlands. In addition, the consortium will commence two new projects, Nederwiek 3 in the Netherlands and LanWin 5 in Germany.

Together, these projects represent a cumulative transmission capacity of 8 GW operating at 525 kV. The projects will enable the transfer of renewable energy generated in the Dutch and German sectors of the North Sea to the onshore power grids.

Under the engineering, procurement, construction and installation scope, L&T will execute the offshore converter platforms and associated infrastructure, while Hitachi Energy will provide its HVDC Light® technology for efficient power conversion and transmission.

Combining L&T’s offshore engineering and project execution expertise with Hitachi Energy’s advanced power transmission capabilities, the consortium is uniquely positioned to deliver reliable HVDC infrastructure that will accelerate Europe’s renewable energy transition and support its decarbonisation goals.

L&T's Offshore Wind business vertical is backed by multidisciplinary engineering expertise through its engineering centre of excellence in India and Sharjah, UAE, strategic global partnerships, a robust supply chain ecosystem and world-class modular fabrication facilities in Kattupalli, India. These strengths enable the delivery of complex offshore structures to the highest standards of safety, quality and sustainability.

This landmark programme further strengthens L&T’s international footprint and positions the company at the forefront of developing sustainable offshore energy infrastructure for a net-zero future.

name: Texas Environment
title: Texas environmentalists seek renewable siting laws, say bans would mean more pollution - Yahoo
description:
Texas environmentalists are urging lawmakers to put smarter renewable energy guardrails in place instead of general restrictions, Inside Climate News reported.
The report's authors argue that without these clear standards, opponents of renewable energy have used conservation issues to stymy clean energy development.
"The massive amount of renewable energy and battery storage in Texas is really helping deliver cleaner air and water," Good said.
Environmental advocates say stopping renewable projects could also pose financial pressures for rural families and food systems.
"Banning renewables doesn't protect our environment," Metzger told Inside Climate News.
text:
Texas environmentalists are urging lawmakers to put smarter renewable energy guardrails in place instead of general restrictions, Inside Climate News reported.

They argue that Texas can protect wildlife, farmland, and private property while continuing to expand wind power, solar energy, and battery storage. Nominal efforts to block those projects in the name of conservation could ultimately push the state backward.

What's happening?

A new report from the Environment Texas Research & Policy Center and the Frontier Group has found that Texas needs science-based statewide standards to define where renewable projects can go and what requirements they must meet, according to Inside Climate News.

The report's authors argue that without these clear standards, opponents of renewable energy have used conservation issues to stymy clean energy development. The topic has previously come into focus at the legislative level.

For example, state Sen. Lois Kolkhorst introduced one proposal that would have required renewable projects to secure permits that other energy projects do not need, while also requiring wind farms to be farther away from property lines.

Separate bills backed by lawmakers including state Rep. Jared Patterson and state Sen. Kevin Sparks would have "sought to force existing wind and solar companies to buy fossil fuel-based power or connect to a battery storage resource to cover the hours the energy plants are not operating," Inside Climate News reported.

Luke Metzger, executive director of the Environment Texas Research & Policy Center, told the news outlet that the better approach is to require best practices that reduce harm to land and wildlife — not to prohibit renewable projects or make them virtually impossible to advance.

Why is this important?

Supporters of developing more clean, sustainable energy systems say the issue is about more than electricity. Ensuring that the application of conservation measures makes good sense also affects air quality, water supplies, and whether ranching and farming families can keep land that's been in their families for generations.

Texas is already the nation's top state for wind and utility-scale solar, and Sierra Club Lone Star Chapter conservation director Cyrus Reed told Inside Climate News that wind, solar, and storage now supply nearly half of the state's electricity on most days.

The outlet also spoke with Quentin Good, a Frontier Group policy analyst and one of the report's authors, who said Texas consumed more electricity between 2018 and 2023 even as power-plant sulfur dioxide emissions fell 50% and greenhouse gas emissions dropped 11%, with renewable growth helping drive that decline.

"The massive amount of renewable energy and battery storage in Texas is really helping deliver cleaner air and water," Good said.

Environmental advocates say stopping renewable projects could also pose financial pressures for rural families and food systems. Without lease income from wind and solar developments, farmers may not be able to afford to keep properties that have been cultivated over generations.

What's being done?

The report proposes statewide siting standards that would be science-based, predictable, and timely instead of relying on blanket restrictions.

That approach would establish baseline local rules, including setbacks, so cities and counties could not use them to effectively block projects altogether.

The report's authors also called for a tiered review process, with tougher scrutiny for projects in environmentally sensitive areas and a quicker path for lower-impact developments.

Garrett Bader, the American Farmland Trust's smart solar specialist in Texas, told Inside Climate News that could mean directing more solar projects to already developed places such as rooftops and carports instead of prime agricultural land.

Lisa Gonzalez, Audubon Texas' vice president and executive director, told the outlet that developers should work with state and federal wildlife agencies before construction begins, adding that responsible developers already use advanced mapping to avoid sensitive habitats.

"Banning renewables doesn't protect our environment," Metzger told Inside Climate News. "It means more pollution, more water strain, and it undermines those landowners that depend on that income to keep their land intact."

“The 50,000th BMW iX3 underscores the capabilities of our plant in Debrecen: Never before have we built so many vehicles so quickly at a new plant.

text:
BMW Group Plant Debrecen has produced its 50,000th BMW iX3, reaching the mark nine months after series production began at the Hungarian site. The company says the figure represents the fastest ramp-up of any new plant in the BMW Group production network. Output was accelerated by a second shift introduced in February 2026, ahead of the original schedule, a step BMW attributes to demand for the first series-production model of the Neue Klasse. The automaker says it is on track to pass 100,000 incoming orders for the model.

Highlights

50,000 BMW iX3 vehicles built at Plant Debrecen within nine months of the start of series production

Second shift introduced in February 2026, earlier than planned, in response to order intake

BMW says it is approaching 100,000 incoming orders for the iX3

40 new or updated models planned across the BMW Group by the end of 2027

A New Architecture Launched at a New Site

The iX3 is the first series-production vehicle built on the Neue Klasse architecture, and Debrecen is the first plant to build it. Launching a new vehicle platform inside a purpose-built facility removes the constraint of adapting an existing line, but it also means the site had no prior production history to draw on.

“The 50,000th BMW iX3 underscores the capabilities of our plant in Debrecen: Never before have we built so many vehicles so quickly at a new plant. This milestone is the result of an outstanding team effort,” said Raymond Wittmann, Member of the Board of Management of BMW AG, responsible for Production.

Hans-Peter Kemser, President and CEO of BMW Group Plant Debrecen, framed the site’s role in similar terms. “The production of the 50,000th BMW iX3 reflects the dedication and expertise of our team. As the home of the first series-produced Neue Klasse model, Plant Debrecen is helping shape the future of the BMW Group’s global production network,” he said.

Why Does the Ramp-Up Pace Matter?

The nine-month figure is a measure of industrial readiness rather than a sales result, but the two are linked. BMW moved to two shifts in February 2026 because order intake for the iX3 ran ahead of the ramp-up plan drawn up before launch. The company says demand has been strong since market launch and that the next threshold it expects to cross is 100,000 incoming orders.

Transferring the Launch Experience

BMW says the Debrecen launch is intended to feed the rest of its manufacturing footprint, which becomes the harder test as Neue Klasse output scales across the group’s production network and into sites that were not built for the architecture.

“Each of our plants benefits from launch experiences we have made at Plant Debrecen. By the end of 2027, we will launch 40 new or updated models. Efficiency, speed, and quality are crucial for the successful launch of all vehicles. Knowledge transfer between our production sites worldwide is a key lever,” said Wittmann.

According to the company, insights from one plant flow into the wider network so that potential quality deviations can be identified before they recur at another site. Digital tools and a shared database underpin the transfer.

title: BMW Plant Woodruff to Power the New BMW iX5 with Gen6 Batteries - Electric Cars Report
description:

Besides Woodruff, Gen6 battery plants are being established in Germany, China and Mexico, while production is already underway in Hungary.
The close proximity between Plant Woodruff and Plant Spartanburg—just 15 miles (24 km) apart—helps reduce logistics costs, improve supply chain resilience and support regional employment.
BMW iX5 Features 800-Volt Technology and Largest Battery Yet The upcoming BMW iX5 will become the first electric X5 powered by BMW’s sixth-generation eDrive technology.
As Plant Woodruff begins volume production, BMW is laying the groundwork for its next generation of electric SUVs in North America.
text:
BMW is entering the next phase of its North American electrification strategy as its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina prepares to begin series production of sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries for the upcoming fully electric BMW iX5 this December.

The new battery assembly facility represents a major investment in BMW’s US manufacturing footprint and will play a central role in supplying batteries for the next generation of electric BMW X models built at nearby Plant Spartanburg.

Equipped with artificial intelligence, digital twins and virtual reality-based training, Plant Woodruff is designed to deliver high-quality battery production while improving manufacturing efficiency.

AI-Powered Manufacturing Sets New Standards

Plant Woodruff has been developed around BMW’s latest Gen6 battery technology, which introduces cylindrical battery cells integrated directly into the battery pack using a cell-to-pack architecture. This design reduces complexity while improving energy density and overall battery performance.

Every stage of production is monitored in real time through an extensive inline quality control system. AI-powered assistants continuously analyse manufacturing data, helping employees identify potential issues before they affect production.

The facility combines the work of more than 300 employees with approximately 250 industrial robots, supporting BMW’s goal of achieving near zero-defect battery manufacturing while maximising production efficiency.

Digital twins—virtual replicas of the production lines—were used throughout the planning process, allowing BMW to optimise operations before production equipment was installed.

Virtual Reality Training Before Employees Reach the Production Line

One of the standout features at Plant Woodruff is its immersive virtual reality training programme.

Before working on the factory floor, every production employee completes training inside a fully digital replica of the facility. Using only a PC and VR headset, workers practise manufacturing procedures in realistic conditions, helping them become familiar with equipment and production workflows before handling actual battery systems.

The approach shortens the learning curve while improving confidence and operational safety.

Built in Just Three Years

Construction of Plant Woodruff has progressed rapidly.

Following the groundbreaking ceremony in June 2023, construction officially began in September of the same year. Manufacturing equipment installation started in September 2024, even before the building was fully completed.

Production preparation began during summer 2025, with test and pre-series batteries already rolling off the assembly line. Full-scale production is scheduled to begin in December 2026, supplying batteries for the all-new BMW iX5.

Lower Carbon Footprint Across Battery Production

BMW has also focused heavily on sustainability throughout its Gen6 battery programme.

The new battery cells contain increased amounts of recycled cobalt, lithium and nickel, while renewable energy is used during the production of battery materials and cell manufacturing.

Compared with BMW’s previous Gen5 battery technology used in the BMW iX, the new cells reduce CO₂-equivalent emissions by approximately 28% per watt-hour.

Plant Woodruff itself operates without fossil fuels during normal production, while hydrogen-powered industrial trucks handle logistics across the facility.

Local Production for Local Vehicles

The South Carolina battery plant is part of BMW’s global “local for local” manufacturing strategy.

Instead of shipping completed batteries across continents, BMW is building battery assembly plants close to vehicle production facilities. Besides Woodruff, Gen6 battery plants are being established in Germany, China and Mexico, while production is already underway in Hungary.

The close proximity between Plant Woodruff and Plant Spartanburg—just 15 miles (24 km) apart—helps reduce logistics costs, improve supply chain resilience and support regional employment.

How BMW Builds Its Gen6 Batteries

Battery assembly begins after incoming battery cells undergo comprehensive quality inspections, including voltage verification.

The cylindrical cells are then grouped into clusters and attached to cooling components to ensure optimal thermal management. Laser cleaning and precision welding connect the battery cells with the contact system, while inline inspection continuously checks every weld.

A specialised foaming process secures and protects the battery components, improving durability and crash safety. The battery housing is then sealed and riveted before BMW installs the Energy Master, the battery’s central control unit.

Every completed battery pack undergoes a comprehensive end-of-line inspection before being shipped to Plant Spartanburg for installation into the new BMW iX5.

BMW iX5 Features 800-Volt Technology and Largest Battery Yet

The upcoming BMW iX5 will become the first electric X5 powered by BMW’s sixth-generation eDrive technology.

The electric SUV features an 800-volt electrical architecture and dual electric motors driving all four wheels through BMW’s xDrive system.

In the United States, the BMW iX5 60 xDrive will be equipped with a 144 kWh net battery, while European models will receive a 141 kWh net battery. This makes it the largest high-voltage battery ever fitted to a fully electric BMW.

Combined with BMW’s new Gen6 battery technology, the iX5 is expected to deliver faster charging, improved efficiency and significantly increased driving range compared with previous BMW electric models.

As Plant Woodruff begins volume production, BMW is laying the groundwork for its next generation of electric SUVs in North America. The combination of advanced battery technology, AI-driven manufacturing and sustainable production methods positions the new facility as a key pillar in the company’s expanding EV strategy.

title: Data center boom sparks lobbying surge - E&E News by POLITICO
authors: Timothy Cama, Katherine Long, Shelby Webb, Nico Portuondo, Sophia Cai, Jason Plautz, James Bikales
description:
It’s a sharp increase from the same quarter in 2025, when fewer than 100 companies and groups reported lobbying on data center matters.
Trump himself praised the data center industry as “real doers” and “an amazing group” during a Washington event celebrating new signers of his pledge.
Greens get in on the action Environmental groups like the Sierra Club were also active on data center lobbying.
They have been supportive of some data center legislation backed by Democrats, including proposals that would set emissions standards for data centers.
The Sierra Club hasn’t come out in support of a nationwide data center moratorium.
text:
The number of companies, associations and advocacy groups lobbying around data center issues more than doubled this spring compared to the same time last year as Congress and the Trump administration sought to address the industry’s rapid growth.

More than 200 entities lobbied between April and June on proposals to prevent data center electric demand from spiking utility rates, a nationwide moratorium on new facilities and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s actions around how to connect the massive electricity users to the grid, a review of new federal lobbying disclosures by POLITICO showed.

It’s a sharp increase from the same quarter in 2025, when fewer than 100 companies and groups reported lobbying on data center matters.

Advertisement

“At this point, almost all my clients are lobbying on this,” said Elizabeth Whitney, who represents electric cooperatives and municipal power utilities as managing principal at the firm Meguire Whitney.

The Washington lobbying rose as concern about the energy and environmental impacts of data centers exploded around the country and action trickled up from city halls and county commission to the White House and Congress, according to the disclosures.

The intense lobbying hasn’t stopped lawmakers and administration officials from acting on data centers, but it’s at least keeping national moratorium demands at bay.

President Donald Trump has gotten hundreds of companies to sign onto a nonbinding pledge that calls for limiting electricity price increases on homeowners. A House committee advanced legislation directing state utility regulators to consider a standard that would put data centers on the hook for the cost of new power generation. And FERC is mulling new regulations.

New York became the first state to enact a moratorium on large-scale data center construction, but congressional leaders from both parties haven’t endorsed the idea of a national halt on such facilities.

Trump himself praised the data center industry as “real doers” and “an amazing group” during a Washington event celebrating new signers of his pledge.

“You have communities that really want the data centers, and frankly, those are the smart communities, because it means tremendous numbers of jobs, very little actual disruption,” the president said last week.

‘Crosses over all industries’

Electric utilities were some of the most prolific federal advocates on data centers, the filings showed, as decision-makers debated how to ensure the grid can handle the projects without increasing other users’ bills.

While companies do not break out their lobbying costs by issue, Pacific Gas and Electric Co. and Southern Co. were the highest lobbying spenders in the energy sector in the second quarter of the year — at $3.5 million and $3.2 million respectively.

Technology companies that rely on the data centers — like Google, Oracle, Microsoft and Intel — disclosed lobbying on the legislation, as did real estate developers and labor unions whose members build them.

“This build-out transcends and crosses over all industries. And it raises many new questions that policymakers had not faced before, while introducing questions into new regions of the country where they didn’t previously exist,” said Matthew Leggett, a lobbyist at the firm K&L Gates who focuses on energy.

Companies are generally supportive of the push by Trump and others to “win the AI race,” said Leggett.

“Investors need to make sure that they get their businesses decisions right, fundamentally. But they also need to make sure that the environment around those business decisions is favorable to those investments and will be over time in a durable way,” he said.

More than 20 companies or groups said they lobbied on executive branch data center action — like FERC’s proposals and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, Trump’s promise that companies will pay for all grid and generation upgrades their data centers need.

Federal interest in data centers took a big step forward last year when Energy Secretary Chris Wright instructed FERC to consider regulating how the facilities interact with the grid.

“What utilities want out of this is an orderly structure that protects their ratepayers, but also allows them to serve these customers in a way that actually does benefit the grid overall,” Whitney said.

On the Hill

In Congress, lawmakers are considering proposals like the Ratepayer Protection Act and the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act.

Meta, Google and the Edison Electric Institute were among the three dozen companies that said they lobbied on the Ratepayer Protection Act, the bill from Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.), Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.) and Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) — H.R. 9340 and S. 5028 — that would direct states to consider whether they need to set new policies to ensure electric rates don’t increase due to data centers.

That legislation has gotten the closest to passage of any major data center bill, getting House Energy and Commerce Committee approval this month. It’s likely to get a full House vote in September, but it’s Senate outlook is more murky.

The Data Center Coalition, which counts Amazon, Google and Microsoft among its members, came out against the latest version of the proposal after lawmakers changed it to target only data centers and not other big electricity users.

Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) — who has championed the bill’s progress — questioned the sector’s strategy on lobbying on the issue general.

“What the data center builders have been not really good at is going and explaining the value to the communities, and so communities want to be protected,” Guthrie said.

“I want them to build their data centers, but I want communities to be protected, and that’s what we tried to strike the balance. I don’t think there’s a scenario where they just do whatever they want.”

The GRID Act, S. 3852, from Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) was mentioned in more than a dozen lobbying filings. It would require new data centers to build their own power generation capacity. It has not gotten much traction on the Hill.

Legislation from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) — S. 4214 and H.R. 9442 — to enact a national moratorium also got significant attention in the filings.

Greens get in on the action

Environmental groups like the Sierra Club were also active on data center lobbying. They have been supportive of some data center legislation backed by Democrats, including proposals that would set emissions standards for data centers.

“Congress has finally started to recognize the massive groundswell of pushback from the public. And as electricity rates are skyrocketing and affordability has come to the forefront for everybody this year — and data centers are a big driver and a big part of that narrative — members of Congress are actually reacting to pressure from their constituents,” said Patrick Drupp, director of climate policy at the Sierra Club.

Food & Water Watch, which has been one of the most outspoken environmental organizations in opposition to data centers and supports a moratorium on construction, said in its quarterly lobbying report that it advocated for a grant program on “data center impact and local capacity.” The group reported spending less than $5,000 on lobbying during the time period.

The Sierra Club hasn’t come out in support of a nationwide data center moratorium. Drupp said the group’s lobbying priorities are mostly around increasing transparency around data centers — like their electricity and water usage.

That idea has bipartisan backing. The U.S. Energy Information Administration has started gathering some energy statistics on data centers, while Texas Republican Rep. Chip Roy’s Public Oversight of Water and Energy Reporting Act, H.R. 9019, would institute a range of new disclosure requirements.

“We don’t know a lot about their electricity use, how they’re deploying backup power, their water usage, their noise impacts — all of these different things that people are concerned about,” Drupp said.

title: Boulder asks the Supreme Court to keep its climate lawsuit alive - E&E News by POLITICO
description:
The governments are asking the court to reject the industry’s bid to overturn a 2025 Colorado Supreme Court decision that allowed the lawsuit to proceed in state court.
Advertisement Exxon, Suncor and others assert that using state tort law to address global climate change is incompatible with the Constitution.
In their brief, the Colorado governments acknowledged that they may face challenges in proving a cause and effect between fossil fuels and local climate change impacts.
“Nor does the global nature of climate alteration disable states from redressing in-state harms.” The brief called oil and gas companies “impatient,” noting that Congress is considering legislation to provide the industry immunity from climate lawsuits.
The U.S. Supreme Court also asked each side to consider whether the court has the authority to hear the case, which has not yet reached a final resolution in the Colorado courts.
text:
Two Colorado communities are asking the Supreme Court to allow them to continue suing fossil fuel producers for climate change, saying the lawsuit is an “exercise of traditional state power.”

In a brief filed Monday, the city and county of Boulder outlined their arguments in Suncor v. Boulder, a blockbuster climate case the court will take up in the fall that could derail nearly two dozen similar lawsuits against the oil and gas industry.

The governments are asking the court to reject the industry’s bid to overturn a 2025 Colorado Supreme Court decision that allowed the lawsuit to proceed in state court.

Advertisement

Exxon, Suncor and others assert that using state tort law to address global climate change is incompatible with the Constitution.

But the local governments say that argument would “cast a shadow over laws long understood to represent valid exercises of the states’ constitutionally reserved powers.” The quote is from a 2023 Supreme Court decision that rejected a challenge to a California law setting spacing requirements for sows.

“Since the Founding, courts have applied state law to such cases, including to remedy environmental harms,” the governments wrote in the brief.

The city and county of Boulder sued major oil producers in 2018, accusing them of deceiving the public about the danger of burning fossil fuels. The lawsuit seeks compensation for the public costs of rising tides and intensifying storms.

In their brief, the Colorado governments acknowledged that they may face challenges in proving a cause and effect between fossil fuels and local climate change impacts.

But “that is no reason to take the case out of state hands,” they added. “Nor does the global nature of climate alteration disable states from redressing in-state harms.”

The brief called oil and gas companies “impatient,” noting that Congress is considering legislation to provide the industry immunity from climate lawsuits.

“Unwilling to let either the federal legislative or the state judicial process play out, they have run to this Court at the case’s outset,” the governments wrote.

The companies have argued the Clean Air Act preempts the lawsuits by creating a system to regulate air quality. The lawsuits, they assert, “undermine that scheme by subverting the primacy of federal regulation.”

But the governments said the Act regulates point-source emissions, not the production, sale or marketing of products.

“It certainly does not charge the EPA with regulating deceptive marketing of fossil fuels,” the governments wrote.

The U.S. Supreme Court also asked each side to consider whether the court has the authority to hear the case, which has not yet reached a final resolution in the Colorado courts. Some analysts suggested the question could signal that the justices want to wait until a final trial and exhaustion of state appeals.

The city and county of Boulder argued the court can only review state courts’ final judgments, “not interlocutory rulings like this one.”

The governments noted the Colorado Supreme Court “merely declined to dismiss” the lawsuit and that the governments “must still prove their claims and overcome numerous other defenses.”

The companies in May argued that the Supreme Court has jurisdiction because the Colorado decision will force the companies “to incur monetary costs as a result of being forced to continue defending these lawsuits.”

But the governments said “continued litigation costs are a byproduct of the suit itself, not a cognizable injury.”

text:
Massachusetts is extending its residential peak demand VPP program to vehicles next. The US state’s ConnectedSolutions program already includes school buses and commercial vehicles in limited amounts, but now it seeks to include residential V2G connections.

The ConnectedSolutions VPP operates across several New England states, including Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire. It aggregates residential devices such as thermostats, water heaters, and batteries, while commercial participants can enroll custom industrial equipment.

Massachusetts already has more than 150,000 electric vehicles on the road. If they averaged 75 kWh each, they would total just over 12 GWh. As of June 2026, the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) sees just under 1.6 GWh of energy storage deployed across the state.

The V2G program will pay car owners that participate in the program similarly to how it already pays home batteries. For example, Mass Save lists a residential battery rate of $275 per average kilowatt of summer event contribution. This leads to potentially $1,375 to $2,750 for residential participants. A spokesperson for the program told EV website electrek.co initially eligible vehicles include the Ford F-150 Lightning, Nissan Leaf, Kia EV9, Polestar 3, and Volvo EX90.

The Mobility House, EnergyHub, and Sunrun are participating in the program. The Mobility House helped the state deploy bidirectional chargers across residential, school bus, municipal, and commercial sites (see flag 5). EnergyHub’s Edge DERMS platform will manage dispatch for the pilot program. Sunrun currently offers a V2G program with Ford F-150 Lightning owners.

Program administrators have not disclosed further details about the pilot.

Per preliminary program administrator data filed with the Massachusetts Energy Efficiency Advisory Council, more than $5.4 million was paid to 5,251 residential battery participants for the 2025 season.

ConnectedSolutions operates alongside the state’s Clean Peak Energy Standard, and enrolled batteries can qualify under both programs.

Batteries in the ConnectedSolutions program delivered roughly 40 MW of net summer capacity savings in Massachusetts during the 2025 season. 28.9 MW of the capacity came from residential systems, with almost 11 MW from commercial batteries. The program administrators’ 2025-2027 plan targets roughly 125 MW of battery performance capacity, with 93 MW residential and 31.5 MW commercial.

National Grid is already testing buses in its V2G program in Massachusetts. School buses, with their large batteries, unique use cases, and finance complexities, have been getting tested for V2G connection for years.

During a June 2024 heat wave, utilities reported that the region-wide ConnectedSolutions VPP reduced peak demand on the New England power grid by more than 375 MW. Distributed batteries have been helping New England consumers reduce energy costs for years, including returning hundreds of thousands of dollars to Vermont participants in the 2010s.

text:
BMW Group’s new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina will start series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries for the fully electric BMW iX5 in December 2026. The AI- and robot-supported plant produces 800-volt, cell-to-pack batteries with up to 144 kWh capacity, using more secondary battery materials than previous generations.

BMW Group’s new plant in Woodruff, South Carolina, will begin series production of high-voltage batteries for the fully electric BMW iX5 in December.

The company gave media a first look at the facility as part of the iX5’s world premiere. The plant uses artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins and virtual reality (VR) applications across its manufacturing processes.

According to Raymond Wittman, member of the board of management of BMW AG responsible for production, “Plant Woodruff plays a key role in the ramp-up of electromobility in the US.” He adds: “With our Gen6 high-voltage battery, we’re not only taking a major technological leap – we are also setting new standards in production. In Woodruff, we are combining cutting-edge processes, artificial intelligence and the expertise of our employees to create a production facility designed for the highest quality.”

The plant’s sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage battery uses cylindrical round cells integrated directly into the battery pack, based on a “cell-to-pack” design. Production steps are monitored inline and documented in real time, with in-house developed AI assistants and agents analyzing the data. More than 300 employees and 250 robots work at the site.

Assembly begins with incoming cell inspection, including voltage checks, followed by cell clustering, where cells are connected to coolers for insulation and cooling. The cell clusters and contact system are then laser-cleaned and welded, with inline inspection monitoring each weld seam. A foaming process protects the components as a single mechanical unit before the housing is closed, sealed and riveted. The Energy Master control unit is installed in the final assembly step, and each battery undergoes a 100 percent end-of-line inspection. Finished batteries travel 15 miles to BMW’s Plant Spartanburg.

The Gen6 cells use a higher proportion of secondary materials in their cobalt, lithium and nickel content, and renewable energy is used in anode, cathode and cell manufacturing. BMW says CO2e emissions per watt-hour are around 28 percent lower than the Gen5 cell used in the BMW iX. Plant Woodruff does not use fossil fuels during normal operations, and its industrial trucks run on hydrogen.

The BMW iX5 60 xDrive’s 800-volt battery has an available energy content of 144 kWh in the US and 141 kWh in the EU (net), which BMW describes as the largest of any fully electric BMW model to date. Propulsion comes from e-drives on both axles via BMW’s xDrive all-wheel-drive system.

Woodruff is one of five new high-voltage battery plants BMW is building near its vehicle plants under a “local for local” strategy, alongside sites in Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Germany; Shenyang, China; and San Luis Potosí, Mexico. A battery plant in Debrecen, Hungary, has been in series production since October 2025.

Robert Engelhorn, president and chief executive of BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC, says: “With Plant Woodruff, we are further expanding our footprint in South Carolina and strengthening the close integration of battery and vehicle production. This creates the ideal foundation for the next generation of fully electric BMW X models assembled at Plant Spartanburg.”

Construction began in September 2023, following a groundbreaking in June 2023. Equipment installation started in September 2024 while construction was still under way, and test and pre-series batteries have been produced since preparations began in summer 2025.

Rich Everly, vice president of production at BMW Group Plant Woodruff, says: “Plant Woodruff demonstrates how quickly we can scale a new battery concept to industrial production. The key factor is the synergy between a skilled and dedicated team and the continuous exchange of experience within the production network.”

title: South Korea to Introduce 'K-Chips Act' Tax Credits for Domestic Production of ... - BigGo Finance
description:
This is the first time tax credit benefits will be provided based on "production volume" rather than investment or research and development (R&D).
According to relevant ministries on the 28th, the government plans to include this domestic production tax credit system in its tax reform proposal to be announced early next month.
The target items have been confirmed as six categories: semiconductors, solar power, secondary batteries, AI robots, wind power, and core materials, parts, and equipment.
For example, the U.S. provides a tax credit of $35 (approximately 51,000 won) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) of battery cells produced domestically.
The government had previously been reluctant to introduce production tax credits due to concerns over tax revenue shortfalls and potential trade friction.
text:
South Korea's government will introduce a "Domestic Production Promotion Tax Credit" starting next year, offering direct tax reductions for companies that produce and sell six key items domestically: semiconductors, secondary batteries, artificial intelligence (AI) robots, solar power, wind power, and core materials, parts, and equipment. This is the first time tax credit benefits will be provided based on "production volume" rather than investment or research and development (R&D). Because it incentivizes production activity itself, similar to the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), it is being called the "K-Chips Act."

According to relevant ministries on the 28th, the government plans to include this domestic production tax credit system in its tax reform proposal to be announced early next month. The target items have been confirmed as six categories: semiconductors, solar power, secondary batteries, AI robots, wind power, and core materials, parts, and equipment. However, electric vehicles, which the automotive industry has strongly lobbied for, were excluded from this round of support.

The credit mechanism works by multiplying the quantity produced and sold domestically by a standard unit price set by the government for each item, then deducting that amount from the corporate or individual income tax owed by the company or sole proprietor. For example, the U.S. provides a tax credit of $35 (approximately 51,000 won) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) of battery cells produced domestically. The South Korean government plans to adopt a fixed-amount credit proportional to production volume, rather than a fixed-rate credit that deducts a certain percentage of production costs.

The Ministry of Economy and Finance had already signaled this approach in its "Second-Half Economic Growth Strategy" announced on the 14th, stating it would use domestic production and sales volume as the benchmark. The standard unit prices and detailed regulations for the six items will be refined in subsequent enforcement decrees. For secondary batteries, it is likely that appropriate unit prices will be set per cell or module, similar to the U.S. approach.

A notable aspect is the separate support plan for loss-making companies. South Korea's three major battery makers — LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI — have mostly been in the red for several years and effectively pay no corporate tax. This creates a blind spot where tax credit-based support alone offers no benefit. The government is reportedly giving serious consideration to providing direct subsidies proportional to production volume for these companies. This is why the government is leaning toward direct fiscal spending rather than tax expenditure through refunds.

The government had previously been reluctant to introduce production tax credits due to concerns over tax revenue shortfalls and potential trade friction. However, as major competitors like the U.S. and Japan race to support domestic production amid global technology hegemony competition, South Korea can no longer ignore the trend. The U.S. provides granular production support, including 7 cents per watt for solar modules, $12 (approximately 18,000 won) per square meter for wafers, and 2 cents per watt for wind turbine blades. Japan also offers tax credits of 18,000 yen (approximately $109.87) per semiconductor image sensor and 50,000 yen (approximately $305.20) per ton of green chemicals, an eco-friendly material.

The government maintains that it has minimized the potential for trade friction by limiting the scope of the Domestic Production Promotion Tax Credit to goods produced and sold within South Korea. It also expects the fiscal burden to be significantly eased, given that record-high "super tax revenues" are forecast through next year.

Kim Bit-maro, a research fellow at the Korea Institute of Public Finance, said, "This is a time when policy responses are needed to ensure Korean companies are not placed in an unfair competitive environment in the global market." He added, "With the low-growth trend becoming entrenched, active support for core growth engines is necessary." He further noted, "Duplication with existing tax systems should be minimized through periodic reassessments of supported sectors."

This tax reform is expected to serve as a powerful incentive to strengthen South Korea's advanced industry supply chains and prevent the offshoring of production. In particular, if subsidies materialize for the loss-making secondary battery industry, it would directly help improve short-term cash flow. However, whether the standard unit prices for each item will be set high enough to meet industry expectations, and whether the system can be maintained stably amid future changes in the tax revenue environment, remain variables to watch.

title: Canadian Solar Unit CS Power Tech Starts First Phase of Indiana Cell Plant
description:
Canadian solar group Canadian Solar is following this trend through its US subsidiary CS Power Tech with a new factory.
New Plant in Jeffersonville Begins Operations CS Power Tech, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar, has commissioned the first expansion phase of a new solar cell plant in Jeffersonville, Indiana.
Canadian Solar Builds on US Market Position CS Power Tech is the US manufacturing arm of Canadian Solar Inc., founded in 2001 and headquartered in Kitchener, Canada.
With the Indiana plant, Canadian Solar adds its own cell manufacturing to its existing US module plant in Mesquite, Texas, reducing its reliance on externally sourced cells.
Canadian Solar Shares Gain Canadian Solar shares reacted positively to the plant opening.
text:
Kitchener — The US solar industry now covers most of its module demand domestically and is increasingly bringing upstream cell manufacturing back onshore as well. Tariffs on Asian imports and the expansion of domestic capacity are driving the reshoring process. Canadian solar group Canadian Solar is following this trend through its US subsidiary CS Power Tech with a new factory.

According to a joint market report by SEIA and Wood Mackenzie, US module manufacturing already covered around 70 percent of domestic installations in 2025, while cell manufacturing — currently at just 3 gigawatts of capacity — remains heavily import-dependent. The US Department of Commerce imposed preliminary countervailing and antidumping duties on cell and module imports from India, Indonesia, and Laos in spring 2026. In 2023, the department had already classified imports from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam as circumventing the China tariffs in place since 2012. Together, the six countries most recently accounted for 78 percent of US cell imports.

New Plant in Jeffersonville Begins Operations

CS Power Tech, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar, has commissioned the first expansion phase of a new solar cell plant in Jeffersonville, Indiana. At full capacity, the facility is designed to produce more than 6 gigawatts (GWp) of heterojunction-based (HJT) solar cells annually, create around 1,200 jobs in manufacturing, technology, and engineering, and represent an investment of nearly USD 1 billion. The cells are intended to supply CS Power Tech's module plant in Mesquite, Texas, creating a more localized, vertically integrated supply chain in the United States. CS Power Tech President Rusty Schmit called the plant a "cornerstone of our strategy to build one of the most advanced energy manufacturing supply chains in North America." According to the company, a second expansion phase is set to begin before the end of the year.

What Makes HJT Cells More Efficient

Heterojunction (HJT) technology combines crystalline silicon with thin layers of amorphous silicon, enabling higher efficiency and better temperature tolerance than conventional cell technologies such as PERC or TOPCon. The cells produced in Jeffersonville are also bifacial and n-type, meaning they capture light from the rear side as well to generate electricity. According to Canadian Solar, this is the first US manufacturing facility for this cell technology.

Canadian Solar Builds on US Market Position

CS Power Tech is the US manufacturing arm of Canadian Solar Inc., founded in 2001 and headquartered in Kitchener, Canada. The group is among the largest solar technology and renewable energy companies worldwide and says it has shipped close to 177 gigawatts of solar modules over the past 25 years. According to the company, CS Power Tech is also the largest manufacturer of silicon solar cells in the United States — a claim made by the company itself and not independently verified. Canadian Solar CEO Colin Parkin framed the investment strategically, saying it demonstrates the group's commitment to "establishing one of the world's most advanced solar cell technologies in the United States at scale." With the Indiana plant, Canadian Solar adds its own cell manufacturing to its existing US module plant in Mesquite, Texas, reducing its reliance on externally sourced cells.

Canadian Solar Shares Gain

Canadian Solar shares reacted positively to the plant opening. The stock, listed on the renewable energy index RENIXX World, rose around 3.1 percent between July 24 and July 27, 2026, to EUR 12.08 (closing price, July 27, 2026, Stuttgart Stock Exchange). On a year-to-date basis, however, the stock remains under pressure, having lost around 41 percent of its value since the start of 2026.

text:
US President Donald Trump visited General Motors‘ Milford Proving Ground in suburban Detroit on Monday, praising the automaker’s domestic expansion and defending the tariff and regulatory policies reshaping the American auto industry.

Trump used the speech to take credit for eliminating the federal EV tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and imposing 25% tariffs on imported vehicles and auto parts — all of which he framed as essential to protecting manufacturing jobs in Michigan.

CEO Mary Barra led Trump on a tour of vehicles spanning several decades of GM production, including the Corvette Z06, Cadillac Escalade V and the electric Hummer, before delivering remarks inside a design facility at the site.

“I’ve done more for you than your parents, ok?” Trump told auto workers, declaring himself a President standing up for the industry “at long last.”

Tariffs as Leverage

Trump framed the 25% Section 232 tariffs on imported vehicles and auto parts as the primary driver behind GM‘s domestic investment push.

“The rule is straightforward: build your trucks or cars outside the United States and you’ll pay a fee for the right to sell them here and profit,” the President stated. “Build your plant in Michigan or anywhere else in America and produce the vehicles right here at home, and you’ll face no tariff at all.”

Trump praised GM for increasing truck and SUV output by 20% so far this year and investing $9 billion over two years in US-based manufacturing.

“They’re coming back home because, frankly, when they build here, there’s no tariff,” the US President added.

“It’s amazing what tariffs are doing for GM,” Trump noted after being guided through a display of vehicles from different eras of the automaker’s history. “They’ve come a long way. The rest of the world doesn’t love me, but that’s ok. It’s called ‘America first.'”

Production Shift

Last June, GM announced a $4 billion investment to shift production of the Chevrolet Blazer and Chevrolet Equinox from Mexico to plants in Spring Hill, Tennessee and Kansas City, Kansas, starting in 2027.

An Orion Township, Michigan plant — previously slated for EV production before demand weakened — will instead produce gas-powered full-size SUVs and light-duty pickup trucks.

Combined, the changes give GM capacity to assemble more than two million vehicles per year in the United States.

Days before Trump’s visit, the Detroit automaker reported second-quarter 2026 results that beat estimates, with adjusted diluted EPS of $3.57 versus a consensus of roughly $3.20.

Management raised full-year adjusted EBIT guidance for the second time this year, to between $14 billion and $16 billion, up from a prior $13.5 billion to $15.5 billion range.

Revenue came in at $48 billion.

[gm revenue]

Policy Changes

Trump reiterated his opposition to EV policies established under the Biden administration, despite standing alongside a CEO who oversaw billions in EV investment.

“On day one, I ended Biden’s insane electric vehicle mandate that would have crushed the US auto industry forever,” the President stated on Monday.

Trump argued that electric vehicles require fewer workers to manufacture — a sensitive point in a state where roughly 300,000 jobs depend on the auto sector.

“And I don’t want to say this in front of Mary, because she’ll change your mind, but it takes far fewer people to build an electric car,” Trump said, referring to Barra. “That doesn’t mean they work better, but it takes less.”

According to the President, “if you want an electric car, they make electric cars, too. But if you want to buy a combustion, if you want to buy anything you want, they make.”

Trump also claimed credit for terminating Biden-era Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards.

“I terminated Biden’s disastrous CAFE Fuel Standards,” he said, noting “that was a short road to bankruptcy for every single car company in this country, and a total disaster that would have killed the internal combustion engine.”

To him, “as long as I’m president, that will never happen.”

Biden-era emissions and fuel-efficiency rules did not explicitly mandate EV production.

Automakers could meet tightened fleet-wide standards through a combination of EVs, hybrids and more efficient combustion engines.

Trump signed legislation repealing the rules as part of broader regulatory rollbacks last year.

Trump also promoted a tax deduction for interest paid on automobile loans, available only for vehicles manufactured in the United States — a provision of his One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

It was under the same legislation that Congress terminated the $7,500 federal tax credit for new EVs and the $4,000 credit for used EVs after September 30, 2025.

Impact on GM’s EV Business

The elimination of the credit triggered a rush of purchases in the third quarter of 2025, followed by steep sales declines.

General Motors delivered a record 66,501 EVs in that quarter, but demand collapsed once the incentive expired.

By the second quarter of 2026, however, EV sales had dropped to 3.8% of the automaker’s US deliveries — down from 6.2% a year earlier.

The company itself flags the One Big Beautiful Bill Act among the regulatory risks to its business.

GM has recorded $7.6 billion in EV-related charges since mid-2025, driven by cancelled supplier contracts, unused equipment and a restructuring of its production footprint.

CFO Paul Jacobson said in March the company was working to settle $4.2 billion in cash payments tied to the restructuring by the end of the second quarter.

Management has temporarily idled Factory Zero — GM‘s flagship EV assembly plant in Detroit — twice since October, permanently laying off roughly half the plant’s workforce.

Production was cut from two shifts to one before the remaining shift was paused.

Despite the scale of the restructuring, Barra has maintained the long-term destination is profitable electric vehicle production.

Former Tesla President Jon McNeill, now a GM board member, said in March the company designed its EVs from the ground up rather than converting existing platforms — differentiating GM from Ford and Stellantis, both of which have taken charges of roughly $20 billion each on their own EV pivots.

Canada Trade Tensions

Trump’s visit coincided with an ongoing trade dispute with Canada.

Last week, he signed three proclamations imposing 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods — including wine, hockey sticks and cement — under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

According to the White House, the provision had not been used in nearly a century. Duties cover roughly $20 billion in Canadian imports and apply regardless of USMCA compliance, with a 30-day implementation window.

Trump described the action as a response to Canadian restrictions on American alcohol, dairy and automotive products.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the tariffs unilateral and said Ottawa had already matched them with countermeasures.

Auto manufacturing has been a central friction point between the two countries.

GM cut approximately 500 jobs at its Oshawa, Ontario plant in January, transferring full-size truck production to Fort Wayne, Indiana.

BrightDrop production was halted at CAMI Assembly in Ontario, affecting over 1,000 workers.

Both moves triggered quota reductions from Ottawa under its surtax remission framework.

Barra has criticised Canada’s tariff deal with China, under which up to 49,000 Chinese-built EVs can enter the country annually at a reduced 6.1% tariff rate.

Barra called the agreement a ‘slippery slope,’ arguing it runs counter to building a strong North American manufacturing base. The United States announced it would not renew the agreement on July 1.

The three countries can engage in annual reviews for the next 10 years until the agreement expires on July 1, 2036 or one gives 6 months notice of withdrawal.
