text:
LFE, industrial intelligence and CE

A new wave of technological innovation is reshaping China’s economic and industrial landscape. Digital technologies, exemplified by big data, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and blockchain, are accelerating innovation, driving industrial transformation, and enabling the transformation of the economic structure42. Industrial robots, as an integrated system encompassing multiple cutting-edge digital technologies, not only reflect the level of industrial intelligence through their application but also exert a positive influence on enhancing production efficiency, optimizing production processes, and improving operational management in enterprises. However, due to insufficient funds, technical limitations, and other factors, many enterprises in China struggle to achieve intelligent upgrading. Local governments’ LFE can play a crucial role in promoting the widespread adoption of industrial robots in production, thereby leveraging their technological effects to reduce CE. Specifically, first, governments’ LFE contribute to enhancing workforce health, knowledge, and skill levels, fostering human capital effects to meet enterprises’ demand for high-quality labor in intelligent production26,27,43,44. This, incentivizes enterprises to invest in and adopt industrial robots, accelerating the intelligent transformation of urban industries. Second, the rise in labor costs driven by LFE accelerates enterprises’ “replacing humans with machines” process45,46,47. LFE allocated to raising minimum wages and perfecting social security systems improves worker welfare while increasing employment costs for enterprises, thereby motivating them to substitute labor with capital factors48. To maintain competitiveness, enterprises prefer investing in intelligent and automated equipment to reduce long-term labor costs. Finally, local governments’ efforts to optimize basic public services have significantly improved the urban business environment49. For local enterprises, this boosts business confidence and increases long-term investment in industrial robot R&D and application50, driving upgrades in industrial robot technology and intelligent production systems. Meanwhile, it is conducive to attracting more external robotics companies and related supporting enterprises into the city51, further elevating the local industrial intelligence level.

At present, the level of industrial intelligence has become a key indicator of a city’s core competitiveness, while the extent to which local enterprises apply industrial robots in their production processes represents the micro-level manifestation of a city’s industrial intelligence. The application of industrial robots profoundly transforms enterprise production models, enabling the efficient allocation of production factors and resources, thereby enhancing production efficiency while reducing resource consumption, ultimately promoting clean production practices52. The root cause of industrial intelligence driving CER lies in green technological progress. On the one hand, industrial robots serve as application carriers for multiple cutting-edge digital technologies, inherently representing the direction of technological advancement while possessing green attributes. On the other hand, the deployment of industrial robots provides superior hardware conditions for innovative activities by enterprise R&D personnel. By leveraging advanced technologies such as intelligent management and smart algorithms, this facilitates breakthroughs in green technologies, extends enterprises’ technological development boundaries in terms of efficiency improvement and carbon emission reduction, and assists enterprises in achieving efficient green technological innovation53,54. Through the application of automation systems with high intelligence and autonomy, as well as the green and clean transformation of traditional production models, industrial intelligence can effectively alleviate issues such as energy waste, redundant investment, or unreasonable investment structures, thereby improving energy efficiency and reducing CE in the production process55.

LFE, market integration and CE

For a long time, China’s rigid administrative divisions have led to the segmentation of factor markets, resulting in losses in factor allocation efficiency. However, inter-regional free flow of factors and resource reallocation driven by local government LFE can effectively alleviate market segmentation and promote market integration. The “voting by foot” theory, proposed by Tiebout56, elucidates the motivation behind labor mobility: when migration is unrestricted, laborers tend to settle in regions that offer higher-quality public services. Consequently, increasing LFE and optimizing the provision of basic public services within local jurisdictions serve as crucial factors in attracting labor inflows. According to enterprise growth and new economic geography theories, local government improvements of people’s livelihoods can promote human capital accumulation, the optimization of the business environment, and enhanced enterprise production performance within the region. This, in turn, increases the rate of return on capital, thereby attracting capital inflows from other areas57. Evidently, the provision of livelihood public services also represents a potential pathway for driving long-term, sustainable capital flows58. Currently, the way local governments compete for production factors has transitioned from low-level, extensive competition primarily based on tax breaks to high-level competition that integrates fiscal incentives, infrastructure development, public services, and other measures59. While fiscal subsidies and tax incentives largely affect only one parameter within a firm’s profit function, government LFE profoundly influences local quality of life and welfare levels through education, healthcare, and other sectors. This approach may prove more effective in attracting high-caliber talent and high-quality capital inflows24. The inflow of factors driven by increased LFE not only stimulates local economic growth but also generates more tax revenue for local governments, which in turn incentivizes governments to further expand LFE, thereby forming a virtuous cycle mechanism.

Regarding the impact of market integration on CE. First, as market integration continues to advance, factor markets are gradually evolving from segmentation to unification and playing a decisive role in resource allocation. The free flow of factors under market integration is conducive to promoting industrial cooperation and division of labor among regions, decreasing the degree of industrial homogeneity, and enhancing the efficient allocation of production factors and corporate productivity. The industrial division of labor contributes to the formation of economies of scale, effectively reducing resource waste in production processes, increasing resource utilization rates, and minimizing unnecessary CE caused by homogeneous production. Secondly, high-quality talent, superior capital, and advanced technology are crucial elements for urban transformation. Market integration lays a solid market foundation for cities to attract talent, capital, and other factors and form high-quality factor agglomeration. Notably, under market integration, the positive spillover effects of technological innovation are more pronounced, facilitating coordinated carbon emission reduction efforts across regions60. Finally, market integration is expected to strengthen the market competition effect. Since some high-polluting, high-energy-consuming, and low-efficiency enterprises lack core competitiveness in market competition, they struggle to sustain operations under the dual pressures of technological backwardness and insufficient funding, ultimately being forced to exit the market. This drives more production factors concentrating on high-efficiency enterprises, thereby enhancing regional energy utilization rates and productivity levels while also achieving regional CER61,62. Thus, according to the above analysis, this paper proposes the following hypotheses:

H1. LFE can promote urban CER to address climate change.

H2. LFE drives industrial intelligence transformation by promoting the widespread adoption of industrial robots, thereby achieving urban CER.

H3. LFE mainly advances market integration by facilitating the flow and reallocation of factors, thereby reducing urban CE.

The Impact of LFE on CE under regional competition

In China’s unique political evaluation system, GDP serves as the key performance criterion for assessing the achievements of local officials, which significantly influences their prospects for political advancement. The promotion tournament theory reveals that economic competition among local governments exerts profound influence on fiscal expenditure structures, infrastructure development, and industrial growth within their jurisdictions. The specific pathways through which local government competition affects the carbon reduction effectiveness of the LFE are as follows:

On the one hand, local government competition exerts a crowding-out effect on LFE. Fiscal expenditures serve as the primary means for local officials to participate in the GDP tournament. Under the dual pressures of economic growth and political advancement, competition among local governments leads to irrational and short-sighted fiscal spending behavior, thereby distorting the structure of fiscal expenditures63. Local governments, in pursuit of greater economic benefits, tend to concentrate fiscal expenditure on productive sectors. Under a fiscal expenditure pattern characterized by “prioritizing production over livelihood”, excessive and repetitive investment generate numerous negative consequences, including resource waste, increased pollution emissions, low fiscal expenditure efficiency, and declines in livelihood welfare64. Specifically, local governments’ excessive investment in infrastructure, such as energy, transportation, and other sectors, exhibits a carbon lock-in effect. The construction process of these facilities is characterized by high energy consumption and emissions, and once completed, they typically serve existing high-carbon industrial systems. This locks cities’ energy consumption structures and industrial production models onto high-carbon pathways. Simultaneously, owing to the crowding-out of LFE, human capital accumulation remains insufficient, failing to provide adequate support for industrial upgrading. Consequently, local economic development becomes locked into capital-intensive yet relatively low-technology manufacturing paths, making industrial restructuring difficult and keeping CE at persistently high levels.

On the other hand, there is the impact of economic competition among local governments on enterprises. Local governments typically employ fiscal incentives and infrastructure improvements as supportive measures to attract external enterprises to invest and establish operations65,66,67. However, some regions, striving for rapid economic growth in the short term, may exhibit regulatory laxity and policy abuse. Local governments may tacitly approve low-end manufacturing enterprises to package themselves as high-tech enterprises to secure fiscal subsidies68. While this may temporarily attract more external enterprises and stimulate local economic development, it exacerbates the disorderly agglomeration of low-end manufacturing industries, hinders industrial structure upgrading and productivity improvements, and leads to higher CE. For local enterprises, local governments may adopt fiscal measures to protect them and prevent their exit from the local market, aiming to safeguard the local tax base and increase employment rates. This enables low-productivity enterprises and even those on the verge of bankruptcy to continue to survive69,70. Such protective measures may also dampen local enterprises’ willingness to compete in the market, inhibit their drive for technological innovation and transformation, and hinder further productivity gains and emission reduction.

The Impact of LFE on CE under regional inequality

Since the reform and opening-up, China’s economy has undergone rapid development, and government fiscal expenditures have continued to expand. As a result, the basic public service system is becoming increasingly robust, the level of equalization is constantly improving, and the capacity to ensure service provision is being comprehensively enhanced. People’s demands for basic public services are also gradually transforming from “having the opportunity to enjoy” to “enjoying more, fairer, and higher-quality services”71. The provision of basic public services primarily relies on local LFE. However, due to the persistent issues of unbalanced and inadequate regional development in China, significant disparities still exist in the fiscal revenue and expenditure capacities of different regions, resulting in a notable degree of inequality in LFE72. Inequality in LFE can exacerbate social inequality and widen the wealth gap, thereby constraining the coordinated and high-quality development of the regional economy, and ultimately hindering China’s progress toward common prosperity. Given this, this paper argues that the CER effectiveness of LFE is negatively impacted by its degree of inequality. The primary reason is that the inequality of LFE exacerbates the siphoning effect of large cities on surrounding cities. As mentioned earlier, LFE can promote the flow and reallocation of factor resources, advancing market integration. However, due to regional inequality, central cities, large cities, and relatively economically developed cities can attract more elements and resources by increasing LFE and optimizing basic public services, thereby creating a siphoning effect on surrounding cities. Consequently, non-central cities, medium-sized and small cities, and relatively economically underdeveloped cities experience limited returns on their fiscal expenditures. This implies that even if these cities increase LFE and optimize public services, their ability to attract high-quality talent and capital remains constrained in the short term due to endowment differences.

Furthermore, some detailed implications of LFE inequality may include: First, when selecting locations, enterprises consider the level of public services for people’s livelihood. In cities with higher LFE, enterprises face stricter environmental standards and higher compliance costs, but they also gain access to more green technology support and subsidies, which contribute to promoting CER. Conversely, in cities with lower LFE, some high-pollution, high-energy-consumption enterprises may relocate to avoid environmental costs, thereby turning these cities into areas with high CE levels. Due to significant deficiencies in green technology R&D subsidies and attracting high-quality talent in cities with lower LFE, coupled with the impact of labor outflow, human capital cannot accumulate effectively. This ultimately leads to insufficient technological innovation motivation among polluting enterprises, making it difficult for them to achieve a clean production transformation in the short term. Thus, expenditure inequality distorts enterprise location choices, causing CE to “leak” from high-spending to low-spending cities, thereby weakening overall carbon emission reduction effectiveness. Second, interregional flows of knowledge and technology are impeded, which is not conducive to innovation sharing and technological progress73. Cities with higher LFE tend to possess superior institutional environments. This provides a solid foundation for the agglomeration of high-tech enterprises and other innovation factors, thereby promoting the construction of science and technology innovation hubs. Under the influence of LFE inequality, innovation activities are primarily concentrated in high-spending cities, while knowledge spillovers and technology diffusion to low-spending cities remain limited, exacerbating the technological divide between cities. Consequently, in low-spending cities, production technology levels remain relatively backward. Combined with the lack of green technology, R&D subsidies and high-quality talent, this makes it difficult to effectively reduce CE.

Accordingly, based on the above analysis, the following hypothesis is proposed:

H4. Local government competition and LFE inequality have negative constraint effects, which can weaken the CER effect of LFE.

Figure 1 illustrates the complete process by which LFE influences urban CE.

Analysis of the current situation

The expansion of local government LFE can significantly improve the provision of basic public services in China and strongly guarantee people’s basic rights to enjoy social resources such as education, medical care, social security, and scientific and technological services. Figure 2 illustrates the spatial and temporal distribution characteristics of LFE from 2008 to 2020, focusing on both the growth of the LFE scale and changes in LFE structure. In terms of changes in expenditure scale, the level of LFE during the sample period has increased substantially. In 2008, most cities in China were still at a relatively low level of LFE. Except for the four municipalities directly under the central government, only a few regional central cities reached medium or higher expenditure levels, such as Guangzhou, Wuhan, Chengdu, Hangzhou, and Shenyang. Additionally, the overall expenditure level across the country exhibited an “east high, west low” distribution pattern. By 2020, with the sustained economic growth, the LFE levels in all regions of the country had increased markedly, but the “higher in the east and lower in the west” distribution pattern remained unchanged. From the perspective of changes in the expenditure structure, the proportion of LFE in total fiscal expenditure has also increased to a certain extent. This indicates that since 2008, local governments have gradually increased their emphasis on the provision of public goods such as education, medical care, and social security. However, due to the pressure of economic growth and political promotion, local government officials have been unable to devote more energy to improving livelihood welfare, resulting in a relatively slow increase in the proportion of LFE.

Benchmark regression analysis

Table 1 reports the benchmark regression results examining the impact of LFE on CE. In columns (1) and (2), the coefficients for LFE are –0.15 and –0.188, respectively, and both are statistically significant at the 1% level. This indicates that regardless of whether control variables are included, LFE significantly reduces urban CE. For every one percentage point increase in LFE, urban CE decreases by an average of 0.188%. Thus, the direct impact of LFE on urban CE is confirmed, preliminarily validating H1. This conclusion provides clear, targeted evidence for local governments to increase LFE, optimize public service provision, and steadily promote CER, thereby facilitating urban low-carbon transformation and contributing to the achievement of the “dual carbon” goal, and responding to global climate change. Additionally, considering the potential lag effect of LFE on CE, we introduce one-period and two-period lags of LFE. As shown in the regression results of columns (3) and (4), the coefficients of lagged LFE are both significantly negative, indicating that LFE exerts a long-term influence on CE. Finally, this study conducts regression analyses on various components of LFE. The results indicate that the coefficients for EDU, MED, SEC, and SCI are –0.167, –0.051, –0.028, and –0.043, respectively, all of which are statistically significant and negative. This reaffirms the CER effect of LFE and enhances the robustness of the baseline findings.

Endogeneity discussion

The benchmark regression in this study may have potential endogeneity issues stemming from omitted variables, reverse causality, and other factors. To test for endogeneity in the core explanatory variable LFE, we conduct a Hausman test. The results strongly reject the null hypothesis that LFE is exogenous (p < 0.01). Therefore, this paper employs a two-stage least squares (2SLS) regression using instrumental variables to address endogeneity concerns. Here, two instrumental variables are selected. First, drawing on the instrumental variable construction approach of Fisman and Svensson74, the average of LFE across all other cities in the province (excluding this one city) lagged by two periods is adopted as an instrumental variable (IV_live). Generally, cities within the same province exhibit strategic interactions regarding LFE, thus satisfying the correlation assumption. Simultaneously, the CE of a given city is largely unaffected by the LFE of other cities within its province, and the two-period lagged instrument variable is uncorrelated with the current error term, thereby satisfying the exogeneity assumption. Second, following the methodology of Munshi75, we construct an additional instrumental variable using the one-period lagged number of annual extreme precipitation days (IV_erd). This variable is calculated based on the daily city-level precipitation data and the classification standard for rainstorms (daily precipitation exceeding 50 mm). Flooding disasters triggered by extreme precipitation compel local governments to rapidly increase short-term fiscal expenditures on disaster relief and water conservancy. After the disaster response concludes, the corresponding LFE may be elevated to safeguard public welfare. Consequently, the one-period lagged extreme precipitation satisfies the relevance assumption. As a natural phenomenon, extreme precipitation is obviously random and exogenous. The one-period lagged extreme precipitation days cannot directly influence contemporaneous CE and are fundamentally uncorrelated with the current-period error term, thereby strictly guaranteeing the exogeneity of the instrumental variable.

Columns (1) and (2) of Table 2 report the results of the instrumental variable regression. The Kleibergen-Paap rk LM statistics and Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F statistics are 268.229 and 155.436, respectively, passing the under-identification test and weak instrument test. The Hansen J statistic for the over-identification test is 1.084, with a corresponding p value of 0.298, which is greater than 0.1, indicating that all instrumental variables are exogenous. After considering the potential endogeneity between LFE and urban CE, the second-stage regression results demonstrate that the coefficient of LFE on urban CE remains significantly negative, indicating that the conclusions of the benchmark regression are not affected by endogeneity issues, and H1 is further supported. In addition, to ensure the robustness of the endogeneity analysis, this study also employs the System GMM method for estimation. Column (3) reports the estimation results, where the coefficient of the core explanatory variable LFE remains significantly negative at the 1% level, consistent with the instrumental variable regression results.

Robustness test

This paper conducts robustness tests across the following five dimensions:

First, replace the core explanatory variable. The core explanatory variable is replaced with the degree of local government’s preference for LFE (FES), calculated as the proportion of LFE to the total fiscal expenditure. The results in column (1) of Table 3 indicate that a higher degree of local government preference for LFE strengthens its inhibitory effect on CE.

Second, we replace the explained variable. The explained variable is replaced with CE intensity (CI), measured as the ratio of total CE in prefecture-level cities to GDP. The lower the value of this indicator, the less CE is generated per unit of GDP. According to the regression results in column (2), the coefficient of LFE remains significantly negative, indicating a significant reduction in urban CE intensity.

Third, we adjust the sample scope. The 2020 COVID-19 pandemic had a substantial shock on both China and the global economy, resulting in short-term economic stagnation. Given the atypical nature of the 2020 data, which could introduce bias into the full-sample estimation, this paper excludes data from that year in the regression analysis. The regression results in column (3) remain consistent with those of the full sample.

Fourth, we apply winsorization. To avoid the impact of outliers in the sample data on the regression results, this paper conducts a 1% winsorization treatment on both the upper and lower bounds of all continuous variables and re-estimates the model. The regression results, presented in column (4), remain consistent with the benchmark findings.

Finally, we control for policy effects. To accurately identify the causal relationship between LFE and CE, it is necessary to control for the interference of related emission reduction policies. Therefore, this study simultaneously incorporates the pilot policy of low-carbon city (LC), the pilot policy of carbon emission trading (CET), and the national comprehensive demonstration city of energy saving and emission reduction fiscal policy (GF) into the benchmark regression equation to examine whether the implementation of these policies interferes with the core findings of this study. Column (5) regression results indicate that after accounting for policy interference, the low-carbon effect of LFE remains statistically robust.

The above series of robustness tests further validate H1.

Mechanism test

According to the theoretical analysis in the preceding section, this paper further examines the mechanism through which LFE affects CE, focusing primarily on the dimensions of industrial intelligence and market integration.

Table 4 columns (1)–(3) report the results of mechanisms test examining how LFE influences urban CE by promoting industrial intelligence. In column (1), we use the penetration rate of industrial robots as an indicator to measure the level of industrial intelligence and examine its underlying mechanism. The results reveal that LFE significantly increases industrial robot penetration at the 1% statistical level, thereby promoting the intelligent transformation of urban industry, which supports the industrial intelligence influence mechanism. The human capital enhancement and business environment optimization driven by LFE facilitates the adoption of industrial robots in enterprise production, thereby promoting local industrial intelligent transformation. As an amalgamation of numerous transformative frontier technologies, industrial robots profoundly reshape enterprise production models, simultaneously enhancing productivity, improving resource efficiency, optimizing production processes, and reducing CE.

Furthermore, this paper posits that the green technology effect induced by industrial intelligence is the intrinsic reason through which it facilitates urban CER. Therefore, a more detailed analysis of the industrial intelligence impact mechanism is warranted. This paper integrates green technological progress into the analytical framework, measured through two indicators: green technological innovation capacity and energy efficiency. Column (2) presents the results of the mechanism test for green technological innovation capacity. We find that LFE accelerates the widespread adoption of industrial robots, providing enterprises with superior hardware foundations and intelligent technological support for innovation. This facilitates the enhancement of local enterprises’ capacity for green technological innovation. Thus, the mechanism of green technological innovation capacity is validated. Column (3) reports the results of the mechanism test for energy efficiency. As shown, the coefficient for LFE is significantly positive, indicating that it promotes energy efficiency improvement. This implies that the intelligent transformation driven by industrial robot adoption profoundly reshapes the entire production process, achieving a win-win outcome of energy savings and productivity gains. Such findings validate the existence of the energy efficiency impact mechanism.

The above test results clarify the process of LFE affecting urban CE through the path of industrial intelligence, confirming the role of industrial intelligent transformation and its green technology impact in reducing CE, thereby validating H2.

Columns (4) and (5) of Table 4 report the results of the mechanism analysis for market integration. In column (4), LFE significantly reduces labor market segmentation among cities nationwide and promotes labor market integration. This implies that the cross-regional labor mobility facilitated by LFE, particularly the movement of highly qualified and skilled talent, contributes to the optimal allocation of labor resources and the upgrading of human capital. Column (5) shows that LFE significantly reduces capital market segmentation among different regions, promoting capital market integration. Improvements in urban livelihoods exert a positive influence on attracting high-quality capital inflows, which not only bring new funds to local areas but also often introduce new technologies. Overall, the optimization of public services brought about by LFE can stimulate the free flow of production factors, reduce barriers between regions to a certain extent, and thereby advance the process of market integration and the construction of a unified national market. Under the process of factor market integration, the more efficient allocation of labor and capital facilitates the dissemination and exchange of cutting-edge theoretical knowledge and advanced technologies across regions, thereby establishing a knowledge-sharing mechanism, amplifying technology spillover effects, and contributing to urban CER.

The above test results delineate the process through which LFE influences urban CE by facilitating factor mobility and mitigating market segmentation, confirming the positive role of market integration in driving urban CER. H3 is verified.

Additionally, it should be noted that the potential lagged effects of LFE on industrial intelligence and market integration may compromise the robustness of the mechanism test results. Therefore, we include the one-period-lagged LFE in the regression analysis. The results reveal that the coefficient of L.LFE aligns strongly with the mechanism test findings, reaffirming H2 and H3. Due to space constraints, detailed results are presented in Table S1 of the supplementary information.

Heterogeneity analysis

First, consider different stages of economic development. Since the reform and opening-up, China has achieved rapid GDP growth through extensive development, but the provision of public services for people’s livelihood has lagged behind economic development. After 2011, China’s economy gradually shifted from high-speed growth to medium-high-speed growth, with its development model transitioning from extensive growth based on scale and speed to intensive growth based on quality and efficiency, marking the advent of the New Normal. Accordingly, this paper divides the sample into two periods, 2008–2011 and 2012–2020, to examine the heterogeneous effects of LFE on urban CE during different stages of China’s economic development. According to Fig. 3a, for the period 2008–2011, the coefficient of LFE does not pass the significance test, whereas for the period 2012–2020, the regression coefficient becomes statistically significant. This indicates that before China’s economic development entered the New Normal, the inhibitory effect of LFE on CE was difficult to achieve effectively. Several possible explanations can be offered for the above findings. Under China’s previous extensive development model characterized by high pollution, high energy consumption, and high emissions, local governments were more inclined to increase productive spending and strengthen infrastructure investment to promote rapid GDP growth, thus neglecting livelihood issues. As a result, during this stage, the fiscal expenditure structure was highly distorted, and improvements in livelihood public services lagged behind economic development, preventing LFE from demonstrating a significant low-carbon effect. As the economy entered the New Normal, the Chinese government began to vigorously promote the green transition of its economic development model. Through continuous adjustments in the fiscal expenditures, the level of public services for people’s livelihoods steadily improved. Moreover, benefiting from the ongoing advancement of market economic reforms and the rapid development of intelligent and automated technologies, LFE effectively drove urban CER through technological and market effects during the period from 2012 to 2020.

Second, considering differences in urban resource endowments. China is a vast country, and different cities or regions vary greatly in terms of climate, topography, natural resources, and other characteristics. Among these, differences in resource endowments cannot be overlooked in their impact on urban industrial development. Accordingly, this paper attempts to conduct a heterogeneity analysis from the perspective of resource dependence. Following the approach of Meng et al.64, the sample cities are divided into resource-based and non-resource-based cities. Figure 3b presents the results of the heterogeneity test based on resource endowments. For non-resource-based cities, the coefficient of LFE is –0.192, whereas for resource-based cities, the coefficient is –0.139. For every one percentage point increase in LFE, the reduction of CE in non-resource-based cities is 0.053% greater than in resource-based cities. It implies that LFE in non-resource-based cities achieves a stronger CER effect. The possible reasons for this result are as follows: First, at the industrial level, resource-based cities exhibit relatively homogeneous industrial structures, outdated technologies, and higher energy consumption and pollution emissions. Especially due to the slow development of advanced manufacturing and producer service industries, the productivity level of enterprises in resource-based cities and the adoption of clean production are limited, which has weakened the low-carbon effect of LFE. Second, at the factor level, resource-based cities face more severe population loss and are relatively less attractive to various production factors compared to non-resource-based cities. Resource-based cities can attract talent, capital, technology, and other factors by increasing LFE and optimizing public services, thereby promoting the transformation and upgrading of local enterprises to some extent. However, due to disadvantages such as lagging industrial development, ecological degradation, and limited economic growth potential, the CER effect of LFE in resource-based cities is significantly weaker than that in non-resource-based cities.

Third, considering differences in city size. Cities of different sizes exhibit variations in fiscal conditions and public goods provision capabilities. Therefore, it is necessary to analyze the potential heterogeneous effects of LFE on urban CE across different city sizes. Referencing to the 2014 State Council Notice on Adjusting Urban Size Classification Standards, this paper classifies cities with populations exceeding 1 million as large cities and those below 1 million as small and medium-sized cities. Figure 3c illustrates the coefficient differences between the two subsamples. A one-percentage-point increase in LFE reduces CE by 0.211% in large cities and 0.155% in small and medium-sized cities. Evidently, the CER effect of LFE is relatively weaker in small and medium-sized cities. Possible reasons include: First, large cities are typically dominated by service and high-tech industries, which exhibit higher energy efficiency and lower CE intensity. Small and medium-sized cities often rely more heavily on traditional manufacturing and resource extraction sectors. The limited role of LFE in driving industrial transformation in smaller cities results in relatively weaker emissions reduction effects. Second, large cities possess stronger fiscal management capabilities, enabling more precise, efficient, and rational LFE implementation. Small and medium-sized cities, however, may face issues such as the misappropriation of funds and low management efficiency. Third, the negative siphoning effect of large cities on small and medium-sized cities far outweighs the positive spillover effect. Even when small and medium-sized cities increase LFE, their ability to curb CE remains weaker than that of large cities. Fourth, large cities possess greater economic, industrial, and technological advantages in intelligent transformation, leading the process of industrial upgrading ahead of smaller cities. Consequently, their industrial production processes are more efficient and cleaner.

Fourth, considering age differences among principal officials. In China, age is a significant factor influencing the political advancement of local government officials. Generally, when comparing two officials at the same rank, even if their achievements during tenure are comparable, the younger official often holds a greater advantage in promotion. This implicit promotion mechanism incentivizes younger officials to work harder in driving economic development within their jurisdictions. Older officials, with lower promotion expectations, tend to pursue economic performance with reduced intensity. Therefore, we divide the sample into two groups, younger and older mayors, based on the median age of mayors in the sample cities. According to Fig. 3d, the coefficients for LFE in the two subsamples are –0.149 and –0.215, respectively. For every one percentage point increase in LFE, cities with younger mayors exhibit a 0.066% smaller reduction in CER than those with older mayors. This result can be interpreted as follows: First, younger mayors may prioritize economic growth and short-term performance, as evidenced by initiatives such as investment attraction, infrastructure development, and employment promotion. Consequently, fiscal spending is prioritized to support economic development rather than improving people’s livelihood. This may partially crowd out LFE while increasing energy consumption. Older mayors, however, may place greater emphasis on leaving a political legacy, thus focusing more on public welfare and long-term environmental benefits. Second, older mayors possess stronger political networks and bureaucratic support, enabling more effective implementation of LFE and related policies, whereas younger mayors may encounter greater implementation resistance or interdepartmental coordination challenges, resulting in diminished policy effectiveness.

The constraint effects of regional competition and inequality

The above empirical analysis has discussed how LFE can achieve urban CER through the two pathways of industrial intelligence and market integration. However, the process through which LFE exerts its role may be constrained by regional competition and inequality. Table 5 reports the test results. In column (1), the interaction coefficient between LFE and local government competition is 0.01, which is opposite to the coefficient of LFE in the benchmark regression model (–0.188) and is significant at the 1% level. This confirms that local government competition has a significant negative moderating effect. Such competition induces declines in fiscal expenditure efficiency, distortions in fiscal expenditure structure, and local protectionism, thereby constraining the CER effect of LFE. In column (2), the interaction coefficient between LFE and inequality is also significantly positive at the 1% level. This implies that due to the existence of inequality in LFE across different cities in China, the siphoning effect between them is exacerbated, impeding the efficient flow and allocation of production factors, and is detrimental to regional human capital accumulation and knowledge-technology spillovers. Ultimately, this constrains the carbon emission reduction process of LFE. The threshold effect test results in columns (3) and (4) further quantify the constraint effect under varying levels of competition and inequality. When ECU > 0.641 and INEQ > 0.403, the CER effect of LFE is weakened. Consequently, H4 is validated. These research findings identify the obstacles to advancing low-carbon city development through LFE, providing new empirical evidence for China’s fiscal system reform, regional coordinated development, and improving the equity and accessibility of basic public service provision.

Analysis of the spatial spillover effect

Considering that local government LFE not only affects its own CE but may also influence that of neighboring regions, it is necessary to employ spatial econometric methods to explore potential spillover effects. First, we construct an inverse distance spatial weight matrix and conduct spatial autocorrelation tests using the global Moran’s I to satisfy the prerequisites for spatial econometric model application. The test results indicate that both LFE and urban CE exhibit significantly positive global Moran’s I value at the 1% level during the 2008–2020 period. This confirms the presence of positive global spatial autocorrelation for both variables within the sample period. Next, regarding the selection of the spatial econometric model, based on the results of the Hausman, LM, LR, and Wald tests, this study selects the spatial Durbin model with two-way fixed effects as the optimal model for regression estimation. The specific results of the aforementioned tests are shown in Tables S2 and S3. Finally, we employ a partial derivative approach to decompose the spatial effects of LFE on CE into direct, indirect, and total effects. Table 6 reports the test results for spatial spillover effects. Among these, the indirect effect coefficient of LFE is –0.567, which is significant at the 1% level. This indicates that increased LFE in a city effectively reduces CE in neighboring cities, demonstrating a significant spatial spillover effect. According to externality theory, increasing LFE and improving basic public services in a city can generate positive externalities for neighboring cities, thereby increasing the likelihood that residents in neighboring cities can access higher-quality public services. Additionally, drawing on the previous mechanism analysis, the industrial intelligence and market integration driven by LFE in a city can spill over to neighboring cities, thereby promoting their carbon emission reduction processes. Thus, local governments should actively engage in regional cooperation in improving people’s livelihoods and environmental governance to enhance overall social welfare.

Model construction

Firstly, according to the above theoretical analysis, this paper develops the following econometric model to empirically examine the impact of local government LFE on urban CE:

$${CE}_{{it}}={\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}{LFE}_{{it}}+\beta {X}_{{it}}+{\mu }_{i}+{\gamma }_{t}+{\varepsilon }_{{it}}$$

(1)

Where, \({{CE}}_{{it}}\) is the explained variable denoting urban carbon emissions, while \({{LFE}}_{{it}}\) serves as the core explanatory variable denoting the level of livelihood fiscal expenditures. \({X}_{{it}}\) is a set of control variables influencing urban CE. \({\mu }_{i}\) and \({\gamma }_{t}\) denote city fixed effect and year fixed effect, respectively, and \({\varepsilon }_{{it}}\) represents the random disturbance term.

Secondly, to examine the specific impact mechanism of LFE on CE, the following model was constructed based on model (1):

$${M}_{{it}}={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}{{LFE}}_{{it}}+{\beta }_{2}{X}_{{it}}+{\mu }_{i}+{\gamma }_{t}+{\varepsilon }_{{it}}$$

(2)

Among them, \({M}_{{it}}\) is a mechanism variable, which includes a series of variables such as industrial intelligence (ROB) and market integration (SEG).

Finally, the above theoretical analysis reveals that the constraints imposed by regional competition and inequality can weaken the CER effect of LFE. To test this, we construct the following moderation effect model and threshold effect model:

$${{CE}}_{{it}}={\omega }_{0}+{\omega }_{1}{LFE}_{{it}}+{\omega }_{2}{W}_{{it}}+{\omega }_{3}{{LFE}}_{{it}}\times {W}_{{it}}+{\omega }_{4}{X}_{{it}}+{\mu }_{i}+{\gamma }_{t}+{\varepsilon }_{{it}}$$

(3)

$${{CE}}_{{it}}={\eta }_{0}+{\eta }_{1}{{LFE}}_{{it}}\times I\left({thr}\le \tau \right)+{\eta }_{2}{{LFE}}_{{it}}\times I\left({thr} > \tau \right)+{{\eta }_{3}X}_{{it}}+{\mu }_{i}+{\gamma }_{t}+{\varepsilon }_{{it}}$$

(4)

In Eq. (3), \({W}_{{it}}\) is the moderating variable, mainly including local government competition (ECU) and LFE inequality (INEQ). In Eq. (4), \(I\left(\cdot \right)\) is an indicative function. If the condition in parentheses is true, it is assigned to a value of 1, otherwise it is assigned to a value of 0. \(\tau\) is the threshold value to be estimated. \({thr}\) is the threshold variable. Both moderating variables serve as threshold variables simultaneously.

Explained variable

The explained variable in this paper is urban CE, measured using the logarithm of per capita CE. Promoting urban carbon emission reduction and constructing low-carbon cities are key prerequisites for China to achieve its “dual carbon” goal and fulfill its responsibilities in addressing global climate change. Consequently, efforts must be made to remove bottlenecks in the development of a low-carbon economic cycle, optimize and upgrade energy structures and industrial structures, advance the low-carbon transformation of urban development models, and ultimately achieve low-carbon production and consumption patterns.

Core explanatory variable

The core explanatory variable in this study is local government LFE. Government fiscal spending on education, healthcare, social security, and other areas not only serves as a basic safety net for people’s livelihood, upholding social equity, justice, and stable development, but is also closely linked to achieving the goal of equalizing basic public services. Drawing on the classification of LFE by Jia et al.76, this study primarily uses the logarithm of the sum of education expenditure (EDU), medical and healthcare expenditure (MED), social security and employment expenditure (SEC), and science and technology expenditure (SCI) to represent the level of LFE, thereby measuring the extent of urban efforts to improve people’s livelihood. Although these four indicators intuitively reflect the level of livelihood public services in a city, they may still contain certain measurement errors. As discussed below, first, the LFE indicator measures input rather than output, which may result in some discrepancy from the actual effects of livelihood improvements. Moreover, constrained by the availability of prefecture-level city data, it is difficult to precisely measure the output effectiveness of LFE. Second, measurement bias arises from inconsistent statistical methodologies. Local governments may employ differing approaches when compiling fiscal expenditure data. For instance, non-relevant expenditures may be misclassified into certain categories to artificially enhance their statistical presentation.

Mechanism variables

Industrial intelligence (ROB). Following the methodology of Acemoglu and Restrepo77, Wang et al78., this study adopts industrial robot penetration as a proxy for measuring the level of urban industrial intelligence. Given that the IFR data only provide industrial robot installation figures at the national industry level in China, direct city-level data on industrial robot installations are unavailable. To address this limitation, the industry classification provided by IFR is first aligned with the National Economic Industry Classification to estimate the number of industrial robots installed at the subindustry level in China. Using 2008 as the base year, and following the approach of Bartik’s instrumental variable method, this study calculates the penetration of industrial robots in each city based on subindustry-level labor force data from the base year. The formula for calculating robot penetration is as follows:

$${{ROB}}_{{it}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j=1}^{J}\frac{{{labor}}_{i,j,t=2008}}{{{labor}}_{i,t=2008}}\times \frac{{{ROB}}_{{jt}}}{{{labor}}_{j,t=2008}}$$

(5)

Where i, j, and t represent city, industry, and year, respectively. \({{ROB}}_{{jt}}\) represents the number of industrial robots installed nationwide in industry j in year t, \({{labor}}_{j,t=2008}\) is the national employment in industry j in 2008, \({{labor}}_{i,t=2008}\) is the total employment in city i in 2008, and \({{labor}}_{i,j,t=2008}\) represents the employment of industry j in city i in 2008. The underlying logic for constructing Formula (5) proceeds as follows: First, calculate the ratio of employment in industry j in city i in 2008 to the total employment in city i in 2008 to obtain the weight for the industrial robot density of each industry (i.e., \(\frac{{{labor}}_{i,j,t=2008}}{{{labor}}_{i,t=2008}}\)). Second, the national number of industrial robot installations in industry j is divided by the national employment in industry j in 2008 to obtain the industry-level industrial robot density indicator (i.e., \(\frac{{R{OB}}_{{jt}}}{{{labor}}_{j,t=2008}}\)). Third, multiplying these two expressions yields the industrial robot installation density for industry j in city i in year t. Summing the installation densities across all industries derives the overall city-level industrial robot penetration, as expressed in Formula (5).

Moreover, the green technology effect of industrial intelligence serves as a fundamental mechanism influencing carbon emissions; thus, this study incorporates green technological progress into the mechanism analysis. Green technological progress includes two dimensions: green technology innovation capacity and energy efficiency. Referring to the study of Shao et al79., this study uses green technology innovation capacity and energy efficiency as proxies to measure green technological progress. Specifically, green technology innovation capacity directly represents the level of technological advancement in clean production and pollution reduction, whereas energy efficiency captures the green orientation of overall technological progress. Regarding green technology innovation capacity (GI), existing literature often uses R&D investment or patents counts to reflect regional technological innovation capacity. Based on this, this paper adopts the number of green patents to measure regional green technological innovation capacity. Regarding energy efficiency (EE). The higher the output level achieved with the same unit of energy input, the higher the energy utilization efficiency, and vice versa. Higher energy efficiency also signifies a stronger green orientation of regional technological progress. Consistent with standard practice, this study measures energy efficiency as GDP per unit of energy consumption.

Market integration (SEG). The degree of market integration reflects whether the domestic market adheres to the principles of uniform regulations, full competition, high openness, and orderly operation, as well as whether the free flow of factors and efficient allocation of resources have been realized within the market80. Market segmentation can serve as a proxy for measuring the level of market integration. More market segmentation indicates a lower level of market integration, and vice versa. Drawing on existing research, this paper employs the relative price method to measure the degree of market segmentation for labor and capital factors81. The specific measurement process is as follows:

Due to the challenges in obtaining directly comparable cross-sectional prices for labor and capital across various cities, this study utilizes the marginal product of each factor as its proxy price.

First, we define a technology-neutral Cobb-Douglas (C-D) production function:

$${Y}_{{it}}={A}_{{it}}{K}_{{it}}^{\alpha }{L}_{{it}}^{\beta }$$

(6)

Where i and t represent the city and year, respectively; Y denotes output, measured by actual GDP; K represents capital stock, calculated using the perpetual inventory method; L represents labor input, expressed as the number of employees at year-end. By performing a log-linear regression on the production function, we estimate the output elasticity of labor (β) and the output elasticity of capital (α).

Next, the labor price (\({P}_{L,{it}}\)) and capital price (\({P}_{K,{it}}\)) are calculated based on the formulas for marginal product:

$${{MPL}}_{{it}}={P}_{L,{it}}=\beta \times \left(\frac{{Y}_{{it}}}{{L}_{{it}}}\right)$$

(7)

$${{MPK}}_{{it}}={P}_{K,{it}}=\alpha \times \left(\frac{{Y}_{{it}}}{{K}_{{it}}}\right)$$

(8)

Upon obtaining the factor prices, this study constructs city-pairs to measure fluctuations in relative prices. Taking the labor factor as an example, the calculation involves two primary steps.

The first step is to calculate the absolute value of the change in the labor price ratio between cities (\(|{\triangle C}_{L,{ijt}}|\)). The specific calculation formula is:

$$\left|{\triangle C}_{L,{ijt}}\right|=\left|\left({P}_{L,{it}}/{P}_{L,{jt}}\right)-\left({P}_{L,i,t-1}/{P}_{L,j,t-1}\right)\right|$$

(9)

The second step is to eliminate the impact of heterogeneity. To remove spurious price fluctuations caused by national macroeconomic environmental changes, we subtract the annual average relative price change across all city-pairs (\(\left|\overline{{\Delta C}_{L,t}}\right|\)) to obtain the value after removing heterogeneity (\({{q\_labor}}_{{ijt}}\)):

$${{q}_{\_}{labor}}_{{ijt}}=|{\Delta C}_{{ijt}}|-|\overline{{\Delta C}_{L,t}}|$$

(10)

Finally, this study calculates the variance of the relative price fluctuations between a specific city and all other cities as the measure of that city’s degree of labor market segmentation. Considering the barriers to factor mobility posed by geographic space, the inverse of the geographical distance between cities (\({w}_{{ij}}=1/{d}_{{ij}}\)) is introduced as a weight to calculate the weighted variance. Therefore, the formula for the degree of city labor market segmentation is:

$${{{SEG}}_{{\_}}{labor}}_{{it}}={Var}\left({{q}_{\_{labor}}}_{{ijt}},{w}_{{ij}}\right)$$

(11)

A higher value of \({{SEG\_labor}}_{{it}}\) indicates weaker factor price linkage between the city and the external labor market, signifying a higher degree of market segmentation. Similarly, the degree of capital market segmentation can be calculated. Ultimately, this study obtains an annual panel dataset for labor market segmentation (\({{SEG\_labor}}_{{it}}\)) and capital market segmentation (\({{SEG\_capital}}_{{it}}\)) covering 281 cities nationwide.

Moderating variables

The variables related to regional competition and inequality are measured as follows.

First, drawing on the approach of Meng et al.64, regional competition is measured using the degree of GDP competition among local governments (ECU). The calculation formula is:

$${ECU}=\frac{{The}\,{highest}\,{GDP}\,{of}\,{the}\,{neighboring}\,{cities}}{{GDP}\,{of}\,{the}\,{city}}\times \frac{{The}\,{highest}\,{GDP}\,{in}\,{the}\,{provinc}{e}^{{\prime} }s\,{cities}}{{GDP}\,{of}\,{the}\,{city}}$$

(12)

The underlying rationale for this formula is that local governments typically benchmark themselves against more economically advanced cities, either within their immediate geographical vicinity or across the same province. By doing so, they can precisely evaluate their relative economic standing and formulate corresponding strategic decisions to narrow the development gap with these outperforming regions. Therefore, we incorporate both the neighboring-city dimension and intra-provincial city dimension to comprehensively measure the intensity of inter-regional GDP competition.

Second, this paper employs LFE inequality (INEQ) to indicate regional inequality. Referring to the studies of Dagum82, Wu et al.83, the Gini coefficient method is used to measure the degree of inequality in LFE at the provincial level, and the specific formula is as follows:

$${INEQ}=\frac{1}{\phi N\left(N-1\right)}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i > j}^{N}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j=1}^{N}\left|{y}_{j}-{y}_{i}\right|$$

(13)

Where yi and yj are the LFE levels of two prefectural-level cities i and j in the provincial domain, respectively, N is the number of prefecture-level cities under the jurisdiction of the province, and \(\phi\) is the average of municipal LFE levels in the provincial domain. Since Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing, and Tianjin are municipalities directly under the central government, and the statistical data for Qinghai Province is seriously incomplete, the Gini coefficients for the corresponding regions cannot be calculated. Eventually, this paper measures the degree of inequality in livelihood public services in 25 provincial administrative regions and matches it with the city panel data. The larger the value of INEQ, the greater the difference in the level of LFE between cities in that provincial region, and the greater the degree of inequality.

It should be noted that, due to methodological constraints in measurement, this study excludes the four direct-administered municipalities and Qinghai Province (due to missing data) when calculating the inequality of LFE. Consequently, our empirical findings primarily reflect the objective patterns within typical Chinese provinces that comprise multiple prefecture-level cities. As megacities characterized by advanced economic development and highly concentrated fiscal resources, the direct-administered municipalities may exhibit heterogeneity in their internal fiscal coordination and carbon reduction mechanisms compared to ordinary provinces. While excluding these municipal samples ensures the statistical consistency of the inequality metric, it also dictates that caution must be exercised when generalizing the conclusion—that inequality constrains carbon reduction—to a national scale. Future research could leverage micro-level county data to further explore the impact of intra-city fiscal expenditure structures on carbon mitigation in megacities.

Control variables

The following control variables are selected for this study:

Economic development level (PGDP) is represented by real per capita GDP. The Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis reveals an inverted U-shaped relationship between economic growth and environmental pollution84, meaning that as the economy grows, pollution emissions first increase and then decline.

Industrialization degree (IND) is calculated using the following formula: \(G={[({{\rm{Z}}}_{1}/{{\rm{Z}}}_{2})\times ({{\rm{S}}}_{1}/{{\rm{S}}}_{2})]}^{1/2}\). Where \({Z}_{1}\) and \({S}_{1}\) represent the total industrial output value and the number of industrial workers in the city, respectively, while \({Z}_{2}\) and \({S}_{2}\) denote the total social output value and the total number of the social labor force in the city, respectively. \(G\) represents the proportion of the city’s industrial structure, which serves as an effective measure of the degree of urban industrialization. Rapid industrialization has facilitated the expansion of China’s economic scale while simultaneously driving continuous increases in energy consumption. Consequently, the industrial sector has emerged as the primary generator of CE85.

Population agglomeration (POP) is expressed by urban population density. The relationship between population and CE has been extensively discussed, with existing studies indicating that human activities are a significant factor causing ecological degradation and increased CE86,87,88.

Foreign direct investment (FDI) is measured by the ratio of actual foreign capital used in the current year to regional GDP. The pollution-haven and pollution-halo hypotheses suggest that foreign direct investment has a dual impact on the environment89.

Infrastructure development (INFRA) is represented by per capita road area. Infrastructure building significantly impacts urban CE, primarily through pathways such as factor agglomeration and technological innovation90,91.

Financial development (FINAN) is measured by the ratio of the loan balance of financial institutions at the end of the year to GDP. The economic and investment effects driven by financial development may lead to increased energy consumption and pollution emissions92, but simultaneously, its financial support for the renewable energy sector contributes to environmental improvement93.

Human capital (HUM) is represented by the proportion of the population with associate’s degrees, bachelor’s degrees, and higher in a city. Human capital contributes to technological advancement, industrial restructuring, and productivity growth, which holds positive implications for urban low-carbon transformation94.

Urban governance level (GOV) is measured by whether smart city construction is implemented, drawing on the approach of Shu et al.95. Advancing smart city development serves as the core driver for modernizing governance in Chinese cities and is crucial for achieving sustainable development goals96. Thus, the impact of local governments’ urban governance levels on CE cannot be negligible.

Table 7 presents the descriptive statistics of the main variables used in this study. Additionally, we conducted a multicollinearity test. The maximum variance inflation factor (VIF) was 3.83 which is far less than 10, indicating that multicollinearity is not a significant issue in this study.

Data sources

All data utilized in this study are derived from authoritative public databases. Specifically, data on urban carbon emissions are extracted from the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR). This database provides highly reliable and spatially resolved global emission inventories and is extensively adopted in environmental economics research. Regarding the mechanism variable (industrial intelligence), robotics installation data are obtained from the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) database. The IFR dataset currently serves as the most authoritative and standardized source for tracking the deployment of industrial robots across various regions and sectors globally. Additionally, the city-level precipitation data utilized to construct the instrumental variable are obtained from the CHM_PRE V2 dataset provided by the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center. The data for the core explanatory variable (livelihood fiscal expenditure) alongside all other city-level control variables are entirely sourced from the EPS database, drawing specifically from the China City Statistical Yearbook (2009–2021), the China Urban Construction Statistical Yearbook (2009–2021), and the China Urban-Rural Construction Statistical Yearbook (2009–2021). This platform integrates comprehensive macroeconomic and regional statistical data in China, thereby ensuring the accuracy and consistency of our localized variables. For missing data points, linear interpolation was employed to impute the gaps.

title: Braun directs state to revisit coal power plant closures
description:
Mike Braun directed his energy and natural resources secretary to revisit settlements that closed or sought to close coal power plants in Indiana.
The secretary should also revisit agreements between plant operators and the federal Environmental Protection Agency, justice department or environmental groups where the State of Indiana was not a party, the order said.
Braun aligned the need to revisit these closures alongside recent federal backing for coal plants in the state.
Also in June, President Donald Trump announced he’d direct $700 million to refurbishing and building coal power infrastructure, including in Indiana.
Braun also ordered agencies to advocate for “affordable, reliable baseload electric generation” in the federal rulemaking process.
text:
Gov. Mike Braun directed his energy and natural resources secretary to revisit settlements that closed or sought to close coal power plants in Indiana.

Settlements identified in a Friday executive order include those that would close a plant before 50 years of service — described as the average age of retirement for electric generation units in Indiana — or where there was no allegation or finding of wrongdoing.

The secretary should also revisit agreements between plant operators and the federal Environmental Protection Agency, justice department or environmental groups where the State of Indiana was not a party, the order said.

“These consent decrees and settlement agreements should be re-evaluated in light of the current and future need for energy to power existing demand as well as future economic development in Indiana,” the order stated.

The order noted a projected 7 gigawatts-plus of Indiana coal electricity generation retiring or transitioning to another source across the next 12 years, as well as an assessment from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation determining Indiana may not have the electricity resources to keep pace with upcoming demand.

Braun aligned the need to revisit these closures alongside recent federal backing for coal plants in the state.

The Trump administration renewed an emergency order to keep two Indiana coal plants open for a third time in June, despite an energy executive calling one of them “inefficient” and “unreliable” and concerns over high costs transferring to consumers.

The generating stations are now set to remain open through Sept. 19. They’d previously been slated for closure in December last year, days after the Trump administration ordered them to keep operating.

Also in June, President Donald Trump announced he’d direct $700 million to refurbishing and building coal power infrastructure, including in Indiana. Indiana’s Merom Generating Station, operated by Hallador Power Co., was among 14 coal plants nationwide to be “saved.”

A previous Braun executive order, issued in April last year to consider extending coal plants’ operations, said that demand for electricity in Indiana “is now increasing significantly due to data center deployments related to the Artificial Intelligence race, reshoring of manufacturing, and greater consumer electrification.”

His order Friday made mention of no specific plants to be reevaluated but said Suzanne Jaworowski, the state secretary of energy and natural resources, “shall consider” the impact of extending retiring plants’ lifetimes on ratepayers. Braun also ordered agencies to advocate for “affordable, reliable baseload electric generation” in the federal rulemaking process.

title: Trump May Need to Allow Chinese Minerals as US Industry Struggles to Meet 2027 deadline
description:
Washington has been trying to limit such imports for years but has routinely granted companies waivers because the U.S. supply can’t meet the demand.
But the reality is that U.S. minerals companies are nowhere close to meeting domestic needs, according to interviews with 16 industry executives, investors, analysts and policymakers.
Chris Berry, a minerals industry analyst and consultant, said the U.S. industry has little chance ​of producing enough minerals to end waivers by January.
That push for stockpiling irks U.S. minerals companies who say they need defense contractors to place orders with them.
“The defense industry is never going to stop if ⁠you keep giving waivers.” Defense contractors Boeing, General Dynamics Huntington Ingalls Industries , Northrop Grumman and RTX did not respond to requests for comment.
text:
Summary

US minerals, magnet capacity not enough to match demand

Trump has set a January 2027 deadline to block Chinese imports

Waivers may be required while US industry grows further

Defense contractors encouraged to sign more US supply deals

(Reuters) – U.S. President Donald Trump’s push to end Washington’s reliance on Chinese critical minerals by January is colliding with a stark reality: American miners and processors aren’t ready.

Trump has made U.S. mining and processing of critical minerals a national security priority since returning to office, pouring tens of billions of dollars into ​nearly 150 minerals companies to loosen China’s grip on supply chains for weapons and other strategic products.

The defense industry and other manufacturers are now just over five months away from a January 1, 2027, deadline under federal regulations to ‌stop purchasing rare earths, magnets, tungsten, molybdenum and tantalum from China, Russia, Iran or North Korea.

Washington has been trying to limit such imports for years but has routinely granted companies waivers because the U.S. supply can’t meet the demand.

Trump railed against such waivers in a May 10 post on his Truth Social platform, saying: “ALL FEDERAL AGENCIES MUST BUY AMERICAN — NO EXCUSES!” Last Monday, he signed an executive order making it even harder for defense contractors to obtain waivers.

But the reality is that U.S. minerals companies are nowhere close to meeting domestic needs, according to interviews with 16 industry executives, investors, analysts and policymakers.

In 2025, U.S. demand for the most-common type of rare ​earth magnet, for example, was roughly 48,000 metric tons while domestic sources supplied 300 metric tons, according to data from the Arthur D. Little consultancy. U.S. firms are on track to have the capacity to produce 5,000 metric tons by year-end.

Rare earths, ​which are among the 60 minerals considered critical by Washington, must be processed before they are turned into magnets used to make weapons, automobiles, computers and other products.

U.S. firms haven’t produced tungsten since 2015 and ⁠tantalum since 1959. Guardian Metal Resources is working to open a U.S. tungsten mine by 2028, while Lion Rock Resources is developing a tantalum mine in South Dakota, with no timeline for opening.

Chris Berry, a minerals industry analyst and consultant, said the U.S. industry has little chance ​of producing enough minerals to end waivers by January.

“It’s going to take many more years to get the needed infrastructure in the ground to compete,” said Berry.

The United States has reserves of most critical minerals; what it lacks is the capacity to mine and process many of them. ​China grew to dominate the minerals-refining industry in the late 20th century and controls more than 80% of the sector today. The International Energy Agency warned this month that $6.5 trillion of global manufacturing is at risk if Beijing imposes export restrictions on rare earths, as it has periodically in recent years.

Asked for comment, the White House referred to Trump’s executive order, which says waivers can only be issued if a contractor shows an “exhaustive effort” to avoid Chinese material and has a timeline for weaning itself off such supply.

The Pentagon did not respond to requests for comment.

U.S. rare earths investment has been hindered by persistently low prices for many minerals, which ​Washington blames on China subsidizing its producers and flooding the market with cheap products, thus making American projects unprofitable.

China has repeatedly said it abides by World Trade Organization rules on global trade and works to ensure stable markets. A representative for the Chinese embassy in Washington had ​no further comment.

Ucore Rare Metals, a minerals refining startup backed by the Pentagon, has developed a processing technology known as RapidSX that it believes is similar to but faster, cleaner and cheaper than the industry standard solvent extraction.

Ucore had planned to start refining by 2025 but has reworked its plans due to ‌what it says ⁠are changing demands from the Pentagon. It now won’t begin some production until 2027 at the earliest, company CEO Pat Ryan told Reuters.

“Can the entire supply chain be propped up by 2027? Boy, I tell you, that’s a battle,” Ryan said.

TRUMP MOVES TO STOCKPILE IMPORTED MINERALS

The Trump administration in February launched Project Vault, a $12 billion effort to stockpile critical minerals for American manufacturers. Officials acknowledged in April that they will need to initially buy minerals from “anywhere in the world,” including China.

Defense contractor Lockheed Martin has given a list of minerals to the Department of Defense it would like stockpiled, CEO Jim Taiclet said at a conference earlier this month.

That push for stockpiling irks U.S. minerals companies who say they need defense contractors to place orders with them.

“Defense contractors have just assumed they can keep buying Chinese products,” said Nick Myers, CEO of Massachusetts-based Phoenix Tailings, a minerals ​startup that last month received a $500 million Pentagon loan to build ​a processing facility. “The defense industry is never going to stop if ⁠you keep giving waivers.”

Defense contractors Boeing, General Dynamics Huntington Ingalls Industries , Northrop Grumman and RTX did not respond to requests for comment. L3Harris Technologies declined to comment.

DELAYS, UNCERTAINTIES FOR US MINERALS REFINING PROJECTS

The complexity of refining minerals has slowed down U.S. projects.

Partnerships with South Korea, Japan and other allies may offer a bridge for manufacturers until U.S. suppliers can ramp up operations, said Samantha Carl-Yoder of the law and lobbying firm ​Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck.

Among the biggest U.S. companies in the field, MP Materials, which is financially supported by the Pentagon, spent years calibrating its solvent extraction processing equipment, part of what CEO Jim Litinsky described ​as a “painstaking” process.

MP has built a magnet ⁠facility in Texas and said it expects to have some magnets approved for use by its first customer, General Motors, by the end of the year. A separate magnet facility that MP is building for the Pentagon is slated to open in 2028.

In Marion, Indiana, ReElement Technologies plans to process minerals using a technology common in the pharmaceutical industry. Known as chromatography, the technology has never been used to process large volumes of minerals.

ReElement said it aims this year to build the capacity to process 10,000 metric tons of germanium or other minerals. In a statement, ReElement CEO Mark Jensen said the company’s ⁠germanium production is “profitable ​at any volume.” ReElement received a $25 million Pentagon investment earlier this month.

Another company, USA Rare Earth , spent more than five years studying chromatography before pivoting to solvent extraction, ​a source with direct knowledge of the company’s strategy said. USA Rare Earth, which is building a South Carolina magnet facility, declined to comment on its processing research.

Elsewhere, Energy Fuels, which last month received a $725 million Pentagon loan, plans to be processing small amounts of rare earths by the end of the year and 6,000 metric tons annually by 2029. ​It is buying an existing U.S. magnet producer.

Ucore, Energy Fuels and ReElement have each agreed to supply rare earths to magnet maker Vulcan Elements, which is building a North Carolina manufacturing plant, slated to open by 2030.

Reporting by Ernest Scheyder and Jarrett Renshaw; Editing by Veronica Brown and Claudia Parsons

text:
Issue Number: Tax Tip 2024-04

Register to monetize clean energy credits with new online IRS tool

Through new elective payment and transfer options, applicable businesses, tax-exempt organizations or entities such as state, local and tribal governments can take advantage of certain tax credits – even if they don't have taxable income. They can apply these options to certain clean energy and manufacturing credits under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 and the CHIPS Act.

Register online before filing

Before filing a tax return, the applicable business or entity must complete the pre-file registration process to receive a registration number. They can register online with the new IRA/CHIPS Pre-filing Registration Tool. Their registration number must be included on their annual return to make an effective election.

Interested businesses and entities should submit the pre-filing registration request for the tax year in which they will earn the credit. The IRS recommends that eligible entities register as soon as possible after the facility/property is placed in service and at least 120 days before filing a tax return. This allows time for the IRS to review and request any additional information before issuing the registration number before the due date of the return.

If the elective payment amount, together with other tax payments and refundable credits, exceeds income tax liability, the IRS will treat the elective payment amount as an overpayment of tax, which can be refunded or credited to estimated tax for the next tax year.
