title: Engineers flattened a power module into a dinner-plate-sized “pancake,” and it now moves ...
description:
It can easily swap in future wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride or ultra-wide-bandgap materials like gallium oxide as they hit the market.
What ULIS is—and why it’s different Enter NREL’s Ultra-Low Inductance Smart Power Module, or ULIS.
With less resistance, electricity switches faster and cleaner.
It handles high heat easily and switches power fast, reducing long-term maintenance costs.
It can easily swap in future wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride or ultra-wide-bandgap materials like gallium oxide as they hit the market.
text:
Our power grids are hitting a wall. AI data centers are devouring electricity at record speeds. Electric cars, trucks, and high-tech factories are pulling more power than ever before.

Our current infrastructure simply cannot keep up with this massive demand.

The standard fix seems obvious: just build more power plants. But researchers at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) have a smarter idea. Instead of generating more electricity, they want to stop wasting what we already have.

It can easily swap in future wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride or ultra-wide-bandgap materials like gallium oxide as they hit the market.

To do that, they built something remarkable. It looks like a simple dinner plate, but it could change everything.

A power grid under pressure

Think about how electricity travels. It goes through many conversion steps before it powers your home.

Power leaves the plant and hits a local transformer. It travels to a substation, enters your building, and powers your device. At every single step, power electronics control the flow.

These electronics work behind the scenes everywhere, but they are quiet energy thieves.

Tiny amounts of power get lost at every single junction. Across millions of devices and miles of power lines, those tiny losses add up fast. In fact, grid losses in the U.S. average around 5% of total electricity transmitted. That equals billions of wasted dollars each year.

Plugging more generation into a leaky pipeline does not fix the leaks.

What ULIS is—and why it’s different

Enter NREL’s Ultra-Low Inductance Smart Power Module, or ULIS.

This little device uses advanced silicon carbide semiconductors. Because of this, it packs five times the power density of older module designs. It is rated at a massive 1,200 volts and 400 amps.

ULIS can handle heavy-duty jobs anywhere. It can run AI servers, power local grids, support microreactors, and fly in advanced aircraft.

Its real secret weapon is how it handles “parasitic inductance.”

Parasitic inductance is a hidden form of resistance. It slows down changes in electrical current and wastes energy as heat. ULIS cuts this unwanted resistance by seven to nine times compared to top-tier commercial modules.

With less resistance, electricity switches faster and cleaner. You get more usable power without burning extra fuel.

The ‘pancake’ design that made it possible

Traditional power modules stack their parts inside boxy, heavy packages. ULIS throws that old design out the window.

Instead, engineers arranged the circuitry in a flat, octagonal layout. It measures roughly 10 inches across—about the size of a dinner plate. This compact shape packs way more components into a much smaller footprint. It slashes both total size and weight.

Getting to this point took some weird experiments.

Early prototypes looked like hollow cylinders or blooming flowers. While those 3D shapes worked well electrically, they were a nightmare to manufacture. They were far too complex and expensive for real-world use.

Then came a breakthrough from researcher Sarwar Islam. He suggested flattening the whole structure out.

Engineer Shuofeng Zhao designed the module’s unique flux cancellation architecture. He summed up the fix perfectly: “We squished it flat, like a pancake, and suddenly we had a low-cost, high-performing design that was much easier to fabricate.”

That flat layout naturally cancels out magnetic interference, delivering super clean power.

Flexible materials and wireless operation

The physical materials make this design even smarter.

Standard modules bond copper onto heavy, rigid ceramic bases. That setup manages heat well, but it adds unwanted weight and bulk. ULIS replaces ceramic with a flexible polymer called Temprion.

This change lets engineers build a much thinner structure. Even better, it bonds using simple heat and pressure. No exotic, multi-million-dollar factory tooling required.

Manufacturers can build ULIS using standard equipment already on factory floors. This slashes production costs from thousands of dollars per unit down to just a few hundred dollars.

In the hardware world, low cost means fast adoption.

ULIS also operates completely wirelessly. It is controlled and monitored without physical signal cables, making it a self-contained unit.

Engineers can snap these modules together like Lego bricks. They fit into everything from cloud servers to high-altitude jets. NREL even filed a patent for its fast wireless communication protocol.

Where ULIS could make the biggest difference

On the U.S. electrical grid, ULIS can instantly eliminate conversion losses. It handles high heat easily and switches power fast, reducing long-term maintenance costs.

In aviation, weight is everything. Electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft struggle with heavy equipment. ULIS gives them a lightweight converter that fits into tight spaces without sacrificing power.

Looking further ahead, clean energy researchers are working hard on nuclear fusion. Fusion devices require ultra-fast pulses of intense electricity. ULIS’s low resistance makes it a prime candidate for these extreme systems.

What comes next

NREL has already made ULIS available for commercial licensing.

Engineers built this pancake to evolve over time. It can easily swap in future wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride or ultra-wide-bandgap materials like gallium oxide as they hit the market.

This small module delivers big results across the board. Making power electronics smaller, cheaper, and more efficient creates a massive ripple effect. We get cleaner energy, cheaper infrastructure, and hardware ready for the future.

Which brings us back to that simple dinner plate.

Why did engineers spend years perfecting a flat, wireless power disc?

Because the quickest way to solve a global energy crisis isn’t building bigger power plants—it’s stopping energy from leaking out of the system in the first place. This little pancake might just be the quiet key to keeping our high-tech world plugged in.

title: Germany stood 2,600 solar panels dead upright on a Bavarian lake, edge-on to ... - Autonocion.com
description:
On a gravel lake southwest of Munich there are 2,600 panels standing dead upright instead.
The builder is SINN Power, an engineering company based a few miles up the road in Gauting.
SINN Power had been running a smaller vertical pilot at Baden-Baden for more than 18 months before Gilching went in the water.
Even with a second phase already drawn up, another 1.7 megawatts, SINN Power says both stages together will stay under 10 percent.
Whether any of it scales depends on a sentence in German water law that nobody has yet defined.
text:
Every solar farm you have driven past looks about the same from the road. Rows of dark panels tilted up at the sky, angled south, all of them waiting on noon.

On a gravel lake southwest of Munich there are 2,600 panels standing dead upright instead. Edge-on to the sun, facing east and west in long rows, like somebody fenced the water in glass.

That is not a mounting shortcut or an unfinished job. It is the whole design, and the reason for it starts with a German law about how much of a lake you are allowed to keep in the shade.

The site is a working gravel pit at Gilching, in Bavaria’s Starnberg district. The builder is SINN Power, an engineering company based a few miles up the road in Gauting. The array went live on the grid on August 21 last year and had its ribbon cut on October 10, with Bavaria’s Minister-President Markus Söder taken out on a boat to look at it.

Rated capacity is 1.87 megawatts, good for roughly 2 gigawatt-hours a year. That is a small plant, and the claim being made is not about size. SINN Power calls it the world’s first vertical floating solar plant, and Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy has used the same wording in its own energy transition newsletter. pv magazine, which has followed the project since it was announced in April 2024, hedged differently and called it the largest floating plant with vertically mounted panels.

The outfit running it sells crushed rock

The lake belongs to Kies- und Quetschwerk Jais, the gravel and crushing business that dug the hole the water sits in. Its managing director, Gottfried Jais, is a co-investor in the plant, and most of the electricity never leaves the property.

That matters more than it sounds. A gravel works runs crushers, conveyors and pumps, and it runs them in daylight, on weekdays, roughly March through December. Jais told pv magazine the arrangement “does not require any land and adapts perfectly to our production plant.”

So the customer is standing on the shore. No transmission fight, no land lease, no farmer to talk round. The company that owns the water owns the power station and burns most of what it makes.

A vertical panel on open water is a sail

The engineering problem here is a good one. Lay a panel flat on a float and the wind mostly slides over the top of it. Stand it up and you have built a sail on a lake, which is an efficient way to lose a solar farm in a spring storm.

SINN Power’s answer, patented as SKipp, was to stop resisting. Each float carries a keel-like structure hanging up to 5.2 feet (1.6 meters) below the surface, weighted with concrete at the bottom, and the modules are held upright against a cable system rather than a rigid steel frame.

When the wind loads up, the rows lean. pv magazine describes the mounting as built so the modules deflect under load through those cables, shedding wind resistance instead of absorbing it, while the submerged section holds the array steady as the lake level moves.

The rows also sit at least 13 feet (4 meters) apart in open water corridors. That gap does three jobs at once: it lets wind through, it stops one row shading the next, and it leaves the water underneath open to light and air. Austria took the opposite route with the same basic instinct, planting 800 vertical solar crosses on a glacier shaped so the wind scours snow away from them.

None of this arrived untested. SINN Power had been running a smaller vertical pilot at Baden-Baden for more than 18 months before Gilching went in the water.

German law lets you shade 15 percent of a lake and not an inch more

Since January 1, 2023, German water law has permitted floating solar only on artificial or heavily modified water bodies, and it caps any installation at 15 percent of the surface with a minimum 40-meter setback from the bank. The rule lives in section 36 of the Federal Water Resources Act and was written on ecological grounds.

For a flat array that ceiling is brutal arithmetic. Panels lying down cover exactly the area they occupy, so 15 percent of the lake is 15 percent of the possible plant, and that is the end of the conversation.

Stand them up and the shadow gets thin. Gilching covers 4.65 percent of the water. Even with a second phase already drawn up, another 1.7 megawatts, SINN Power says both stages together will stay under 10 percent.

There is a live legal question sitting underneath all of it. Lawyers at the German firm ARQIS have argued that for vertical systems the 15 percent should be measured against the water actually covered rather than the full project footprint, and noted that no German authority or court has ever defined what “cover” means in this context. The Bundesrat asked the federal government to revisit the rule in a resolution passed in September 2025. It has not been changed.

Noon has become the worst hour to sell electricity in Germany

The east-west trick is not only about squeezing past the water rule. It moves when the power arrives.

Panels aimed east and west make less at midday than a south-facing array and more in the morning and evening. In a country carrying roughly 117 gigawatts of solar, that is where the value went.

Germany logged 573 hours of negative day-ahead power prices in 2025, a record, according to Bundesnetzagentur figures, and they bunch up in sunny midday windows when everybody’s panels produce at the same moment. On May 1 this year the German day-ahead price hit the market floor of minus €499.99 per megawatt-hour.

Philipp Sinn, SINN Power’s founder and chief executive, introduced the plant at the opening as “a photovoltaic system that produces electricity when conventional power plants are standing still.” Turn that around and it says the same thing: it produces when everyone else’s solar has already flooded the market.

The federal economy ministry puts the commercially viable floating solar potential on Germany’s artificial lakes at 1.8 gigawatts with south-facing modules and 2.5 gigawatts with east-west ones. Same lakes, same 15 percent rule. Turning the panels sideways is worth about 700 megawatts on its own. Fraunhofer ISE and RWE count 6,043 artificial lakes of at least one hectare in Germany, and roughly 70 percent of them are gravel pits.

The performance numbers are the company’s, and they do not quite agree

SINN Power’s October announcement said the gravel works had cut its grid electricity purchases by close to 60 percent in early operation, with up to 70 percent expected once things settled down. The write-up the company published in November said grid draw fell 70 percent across the first three weeks, a stretch in which the plant made more than 100 megawatt-hours in autumn weather.

Both are self-consumption figures, and it is worth being precise about that. Neither is a panel efficiency number, neither has been independently audited, and the 70 percent describes how much less power the gravel works buys, not how well the panels convert sunlight.

The ecological claims are the company’s as well. SINN Power reports waterfowl nesting on the floats, fish gathering around the concrete ballast where algae form on it, and monitoring buoys showing water quality holding or improving. Independent work on this question does exist elsewhere: a Dutch quarry lake study counted fish and invertebrates under a flat array and found more life than the critics predicted. Nobody outside the company has published on this particular lake.

Nine months in, the delegations started showing up

The freshest thing about the plant is who has been standing on the bank looking at it.

During Intersolar Europe in Munich, June 23 to 25 this year, SINN Power skipped the usual booth routine and drove visitors 20 miles west to the water instead. The company says groups from India, Taiwan, China, Israel and Turkey came out to see it running.

That is the real test of a format record rather than a size record. A 1.87-megawatt plant does not move a national grid. A 1.87-megawatt plant that a Taiwanese delegation flies in to inspect might change what gets built on the next few thousand lakes.

American reservoirs are the version of this argument with the volume turned up. A federal NREL assessment published in February mapped floating solar potential on US federally regulated reservoirs large enough to power tens of millions of homes, on water that already has substations and transmission rights attached. The United States has no 15 percent coverage statute forcing anyone to stand panels on edge. Germany’s constraint is what produced the design.

The second Gilching phase is still in planning. The water rule is still on the books, still undefined for vertical hardware. SINN Power has meanwhile taken the same structural idea to sea, dropping a platform called SOcean into open water off Heraklion, Crete, on May 27 for a multi-month endurance run under a German federal research programme, carrying solar modules and wave energy hardware together.

Whether any of it scales depends on a sentence in German water law that nobody has yet defined. What is already settled is smaller and harder to argue with. The gravel company’s power bill went down, the lake is still a lake, and 2,600 panels have now stood through a Bavarian winter standing straight up.

title: Global Electric Vehicle Market Outlook to 2033
description:
The global electric vehicle market is expanding rapidly.
Valued at around $833.2 billion in 2026, the global electric vehicle market is projected to reach $2,169.5 billion by 2033.
Global Electric Vehicle Market Segmentation Battery electric vehicles are expected to remain the leading propulsion segment.
Asia Pacific Leads the Regional Market Asia Pacific holds the largest share of the electric vehicle market.
Market Summary The global electric vehicle market is projected to grow from US$833.2 billion in 2026 to US$2,169.5 billion by 2033.
text:
The global electric vehicle market is expanding rapidly. Valued at around $833.2 billion in 2026, the global electric vehicle market is projected to reach $2,169.5 billion by 2033. This represents a compound annual growth rate of 14.7%.

Continuous battery technology improvements are supporting this expansion. Other factors include declining battery costs, supportive government policies and strong automotive industry investments.

Electric vehicles are becoming central to transportation decarbonization strategies. They support national climate targets and are reshaping the future of mobility.

Charging infrastructure gaps and affordability challenges remain in some regions. However, lower ownership costs and wider model availability continue to strengthen consumer adoption.

BYD’s Vertical Integration Supports 2025 Growth

A key development in 2025 was BYD’s continued growth, supported by its vertically integrated business model. According to the Financial Times, BYD controls much of its supply chain. Its operations include battery production and other key manufacturing capabilities. This structure reduces the company’s reliance on external suppliers and strengthens production efficiency.

BYD has also expanded its control over logistics, including vehicle transportation. This expansion forms part of its broader integration strategy.

The company’s manufacturing scale continued to accelerate in 2025. BYD sold 1,000,804 new energy vehicles during the first quarter, representing a 59.8% year-over-year increase.

Passenger vehicle sales reached 986,098 units, while commercial vehicle sales totaled 14,706 units. Battery electric vehicle sales reached 416,388 units. Plug-in hybrid vehicle sales totaled 569,710 units.

BYD also reported plans to increase exports from 417,204 vehicles in 2024 to 800,000 vehicles in 2025. The target reflects its growing international ambitions.

The company’s 2025 performance followed record sales of approximately 4.25 million new energy vehicles in 2024. Revenue increased to 777 billion yuan.

These results demonstrate how BYD’s integrated manufacturing approach supports production growth and financial performance. In-house production and expanding global operations have strengthened the company’s competitiveness in international electric vehicle markets.

Government Policies Accelerate EV Adoption

Government incentives and tighter emission standards are increasing global demand for electric vehicles. Policymakers are using subsidies, tax exemptions, purchase incentives and zero-emission mandates. These measures aim to reduce fossil fuel dependence and encourage cleaner transportation alternatives.

Countries across Europe, North America and Asia Pacific are implementing stricter fuel economy regulations. Electrification has therefore become a critical compliance strategy for automakers.

More than 85% of global vehicle sales are covered by increasingly stringent fuel economy and carbon dioxide regulations.

China, the European Union and several U.S. states have strengthened zero-emission vehicle targets. These policies have created a favorable environment for EV manufacturers.

They have also accelerated investments in battery production, vehicle assembly plants and charging infrastructure.

Public and private investments in charging networks are expanding rapidly. Governments are introducing EV charging requirements for new residential and commercial buildings. They are also supporting nationwide fast-charging corridors.

Urban low-emission zones and preferential access policies are encouraging EV ownership in densely populated cities.

China continues to demonstrate the impact of policy-driven growth. The country sold more than 11 million electric vehicles in 2024. That total exceeded global EV sales recorded only a few years earlier.

Government-backed vehicle replacement programs and incentives continue to stimulate demand.

India’s target of 30% EV penetration by 2030 is also driving investment across its domestic EV ecosystem. These initiatives are creating opportunities for automakers, battery manufacturers and charging infrastructure providers.

Battery Advances and Lower Costs Support Demand

Battery technology improvements and lower lifetime ownership costs are also driving the electric vehicle market. Advances in lithium-ion batteries have increased vehicle range and improved energy density. They have also reduced charging times and production costs.

These developments are making EVs more competitive with conventional internal combustion engine vehicles. Electric vehicles can deliver up to 50% lower maintenance and operating costs over their lifetime. This comparison is based on internal combustion engine vehicles.

EVs have fewer moving parts and lower servicing requirements. Reduced fuel expenses also make them more attractive to consumers and commercial operators. Private consumers, fleet operators and transportation providers are increasingly considering these cost advantages.

Manufacturers are also introducing software-defined vehicles, advanced driver assistance systems and connected features. These technologies can enhance the ownership experience.

Continuous innovation is improving vehicle performance while reducing costs. It also supports broader adoption across developed and emerging economies.

Global Electric Vehicle Market Segmentation

Battery electric vehicles are expected to remain the leading propulsion segment. They are projected to account for approximately 45% of the global market. Declining battery costs, expanding charging infrastructure and government incentives support this position. These factors continue to promote zero-emission mobility.

Fuel cell electric vehicles are projected to become the fastest-growing propulsion segment. Growth is expected across long-haul freight, heavy commercial vehicles and industrial transportation.

Fast refueling and extended driving range provide advantages in these applications. Plug-in hybrid electric vehicles continue to serve as a transitional technology. They remain relevant in regions with limited charging infrastructure.

A 2025 development reinforced battery electric vehicle leadership. Major automakers, including BYD and Tesla, expanded battery-powered vehicle portfolios and production capacity.

These investments strengthened global EV supply and accelerated the transition toward fully electric mobility.

Asia Pacific Leads the Regional Market

Asia Pacific holds the largest share of the electric vehicle market. The region accounts for more than 58% of global value. Large-scale manufacturing, strong policy support and expanding consumer adoption support this position.

China leads electric vehicle production and consumption. The country benefits from advanced battery supply chains, cost competitiveness and sustained government incentives.

China’s EV sales surpassed 11 million units in 2024. Electric vehicles represented nearly half of all new vehicle purchases by year-end.

India is emerging as one of the fastest-growing EV markets. The country recorded approximately 50% growth in 2023, with more than 1.5 million units sold.

Government initiatives and domestic battery manufacturing investments support its long-term growth prospects. India’s target of 30% EV penetration by 2030 provides additional support.

Europe remains the second-largest electric vehicle market. Emission regulations and electrification targets continue to sustain demand.

Battery electric vehicles are gaining market share across major European economies. However, policy changes and subsidy withdrawals have created uneven growth in some countries.

North America also remains a key market. Local manufacturing investments, tax incentives and increased competition support regional growth. Competition includes established automakers and emerging EV brands.

Key Players and Business Strategies

Leading market participants include Tesla, BYD, Hyundai Motor Group, Volkswagen Group and SAIC Motor.

Tesla: The company uses aggressive pricing strategies, software capabilities and autonomous driving investments. These measures support its global competitiveness as competition intensifies.

BYD: The company focuses on vertical integration across major parts of its supply chain. This approach reduces costs, secures battery availability and accelerates product launches.

Hyundai Motor Group: The automaker is expanding local manufacturing capacity. It is also using government incentives to strengthen its position in North America and other markets.

Volkswagen Group: The company continues investing in dedicated EV platforms, battery partnerships and large-scale electrification programs. These investments support the expansion of its global electric vehicle portfolio.

SAIC Motor: The company benefits from China’s manufacturing ecosystem and strategic partnerships. These advantages support competitive pricing and expansion in domestic and international markets.

Market Summary

The global electric vehicle market is projected to grow from US$833.2 billion in 2026 to US$2,169.5 billion by 2033. The market is expected to register a compound annual growth rate of 14.7%. Government incentives, stricter emission regulations and battery technology advances continue to accelerate EV adoption.

Battery electric vehicles are expected to lead the propulsion segment with a 45% market share. Fuel cell electric vehicles are projected to become the fastest-growing propulsion technology.

Asia Pacific is projected to represent more than 58% of the global market. China’s manufacturing strength and large-scale adoption support the region’s position.

India is expected to become the fastest-growing regional market.

Embrace the Warmth Both rising energy costs and advances in heating technology mean homeowners are paying more attention to supplemental heat sources.
text:
Secondary heat sources help lower heating costs and provide reliable warmth during colder weather. Modern systems offer cleaner, more efficient performance than older models.

Families trying to manage monthly heating expenses are facing challenges caused by rising energy costs. According to recent data from The Century Foundation, since 2022, the average U.S. consumer’s overdue utility balance increased by 32 percent.

More homeowners are looking for ways to heat their homes efficiently without depending on a single heating system. Secondary heat sources provide not only additional warmth but also more flexibility during colder months.

Today’s modern options combine reliability with improved efficiency and convenience.

What Are the Latest Trends in Home Heating?

The way Americans heat their homes looks different than it did a decade ago. The U.S. Energy Information Administration reports electricity served as the primary heating fuel for 42% of households in 2024, while natural gas accounted for 47%, compared to 49% in 2010.

The changing mix of heating fuels supports home heating trends focused on flexible solutions that work alongside existing systems. Popular options include:

Pellet stove systems

Standalone gas heaters

Ductless heat pumps

How Have Traditional Heat Sources Improved?

The biggest changes in traditional heating happened behind the scenes. Improved materials, smarter controls, and more efficient designs helped update older concepts. For example, improvements make options like a pellet stove easier to use while maintaining its appeal as a reliable heating solution.

Reviving traditional heating methods includes the following advancements:

Cleaner combustion

Remote operation

Safety sensors

Automated controls

Efficient fuel use

What Is the Best Secondary Heat Source?

No single heating option works for every home. Factors like climate, square footage, fuel availability, and lifestyle preferences all influence which alternative heating solutions make the most sense.

Pellet Stoves

A pellet stove provides heat through an automated system that feeds compressed pellets into the unit as needed. The design makes them appealing to homeowners who want traditional warmth with less hands-on maintenance.

Gas Heaters

Gas heaters deliver fast, consistent warmth and work well in spaces that need supplemental heating without a large installation project. If you have ready access to propane or natural gas, a gas heater is a great option for convenience.

Wood Stoves

Electric heaters warm individual rooms without fuel storage or permanent installation requirements. Their compact design makes them useful for bedrooms, offices, and other areas that need targeted heat.

How Can I Heat My Home Without Electricity?

A winter power outage can shut down gas-fueled furnaces, heat pumps, and electric heating systems. There’s no need to panic. Certain gas heaters and pellet stoves continue producing heat even during an outage.

Safety matters when preparing to use alternate heating sources. First, make sure you prepare before severe weather arrives by confirming fuel availability.

Second, follow installation guidelines and maintain proper ventilation to reduce safety risks.

Embrace the Warmth

Both rising energy costs and advances in heating technology mean homeowners are paying more attention to supplemental heat sources. From pellet stoves to gas and electric heaters, you have more choices to improve winter comfort.

Come back again soon and check out our fresh content and news stories. We’re here to help you find more ways to enjoy life.

Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Despite the sharp U-turn in federal energy policy last year, renewable energy continues to rise in the US, particularly in the area of solar power. That helps explain why competition for space in the energy storage industry continues to heat up. Among other recent developments comes word of new activity in the ancient field of flywheels. Yes, flywheels. Initially deployed by potters as far back as 6,000 BC, flywheels are fixtures in aerospace and automotive applications among others, and now they have emerged to support the wind and solar industries.

The Long Duration Energy Storage Race Heats Up

Flywheels are marking out space in the somewhat rarified world of long duration energy storage. Going by a benchmark set by the US Department of Energy, that means a capacity of at least 10 hours, though ideally long duration technology can stretch into multiple days and longer.

To date, pumped hydropower has provided the largest source of utility-scale, long duration energy storage in the US by far, claiming about 95% of the market. With support — somewhat weirdly — from US President Donald Trump’s “American Energy Dominance” policy, pumped storage will almost certainly continue to dominate on a capacity basis. Availability, though, is another question entirely. Pumped storage is an expensive, infrastructure-dependent venture limited by the requisite resources, namely water and elevation.

New developments in the field will eventually extend the availability of pumped storage (here’s an example, and here’s another one). However, for the time being the limitations apply, leaving plenty of room for alternative technologies to fill the gap.

Within that space, there is also room for flywheels. Lithium-ion battery technology has been improving, but not to the extent that it can compete in the long duration market. Other non-battery, long duration alternatives have been emerging, particularly in the thermal field where excess electricity can be deployed to heat specialized bricks or modules. Compressed air storage is another technology to gain currency in recent years. So far, though, scale-up has been slow, leaving an opening for other new systems including flywheels (see more flywheel background here).

The Qnetic Advantage

The latest news in the flywheel space comes from the startup Qnetic. The company, which has headquarters in the US and China, is currently aiming at the market for up to 12 hours of energy storage. The plan is to manufacture the company’s forthcoming Pulsar system in the US, though the company is currently building a testing facility in China, which it is billing as “the world’s largest dedicated flywheel test cell.”

“The purpose-built test facility, located at Qnetic’s Technology Center in Shanghai, represents a million-dollar-plus investment that will serve as the company’s primary site for validating the performance, safety, and reliability of its next-generation flywheel systems,” Qnetic explains.

So far, all is going according to plan. Earlier this month, Qnetic reported that excavation and foundation work at the site is well under way, while work is progressing on a 200 kilowatt-hour Pulsar prototype.

Qnetic expects Pulsar to deliver long duration energy storage at a lifecycle cost lower than lithium-ion technology, while also shaving fire risk down to a minimum and reducing, if not eliminating, supply chain risks related to critical materials.

“Unlike batteries, which store energy chemically, flywheels store energy kinetically by spinning a rotor at extremely high speed inside a vacuum enclosure,” Qnetic explains.

“When electricity is needed, the rotating mass drives a generator to return energy to the grid. Because the process involves no electrochemical reactions, flywheel systems can deliver decades of high-performance operation while offering rapid response,” the company elaborates.

Follow The Money

As for what, exactly, can be expected of the new energy storage system, the company states that a Qnetic project “offers the potential to generate 2X the revenue of an equivalent lithium system, every single day.”

That remains to be seen, but Qnetic also notes that its pre-market regimen includes validation by the independent, global-facing, California-based organization EPRI (Electric Power Research Institute).

In a technology brief posted last October, EPRI described how Qnetic expects to distinguish itself from other competitors in the flywheel field (break added for readability):

“Qnetic Corporation is developing a flywheel energy storage technology that uses a spinning rotor to store kinetic energy. Qnetic’s system uses a 15-foot (4.5m) tall high-speed rotor made from carbon fiber to improve the energy density of the system compared to a lower-speed, heavier rotor.

“This rotor is held in a vacuum and is magnetically levitated by repulsive permanent magnets to eliminate wear and mechanical friction losses, which is a key weakness of current flywheel technologies.”

“Qnetic is planning to first go to market with a 500kWh unit, followed by a unit that stores 1,000kWh of energy to be discharged over 4–12 hours with an 85% round-trip efficiency,” EPRI adds.

That rundown apparently rang some bells within the investor community. In March of this year, Qnetic announced that it raised $7.1 million in a 12-month period, including a $5 million funding round this year and a $2.1 million equity crowdfunding campaign last year.

The funds are earmarked for Qnetic’s forthcoming California factory, beginning with low-volume production of its Q500 energy storage system.

Qnetic also too note of its validation agreement with EPRI, and the company referenced another validation agreement, with the US Department of Energy lab formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.

The NREL connection is of interest considering that the lab produced a report in 2021 exploring some of the assumptions, limitations, and opportunities in the area of hybrid storage systems, including mechanical technologies.

More recently, the Energy Department’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory zeroed in on the potential for lithium-ion batteries to enhance revenue from hydropower systems, with positive results for short-duration batteries of just two hours. Of interest in that regard, the US flywheel startup Torus is already working on a flywheel-battery combo.

PNNL’s award-winning flywheel program could also come into play, so keep an eye out for flywheel-enhanced hydropower to make an appearance somewhere down the line.

Photo: New flywheel energy storage systems can be located largely underground, offering aesthetic benefits alongside the potential for lower costs, longer duration, and less reliance on overseas supply chains (courtesy of Qnetic).

text:
Indiana Michigan Power will soon retire the coal-burning units at its Rockport electric generating plant. The 2,600-megawatt plant is a source of energy, jobs and tax revenue in the southern Indiana community along the Ohio River.

Losing it would be “devastating,” Spencer County Commissioner Jim Seiler said.

“I mean, if they completely close down, that would just kill our schools and our whole area,” he said.

That’s not the plan. I&M, owned by utility giant AEP, wants state regulatory approval for a 1,520-megawatt natural gas-burning facility at the Rockport site. But it’s also evaluating the location for nuclear generation, seeking federal grants to support the approval process for a small modular reactor.

Gov. Mike Braun applauded the effort just days after taking office early last year. Spencer County commissioners, including Seiler, offered their support in a 2024 letter.

“We have to have energy, and it just kind of looks like to me that the nuclear thing — nuclear and gas are the way to go,” Seiler said.

I&M’s efforts could offer a glimpse into what the Braun administration envisions for its oft-mentioned “all-of-the-above approach” to energy and affordability, which is increasingly propping up arguments for nuclear development.

The latest of its efforts is the Indiana Advanced Nuclear Ready Community program, announced last week by Braun, which aims to introduce counties and regions to nuclear energy and attract developers.

The program highlights small modular reactors, like the one AEP is exploring. While they produce about a third of the electricity of a traditional nuclear reactor, they’re smaller and can be more affordable to construct, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency.

But no small modular reactor project has ever been completed in the United States, according to the World Nuclear Association. Just one is under construction in Tennessee, with several more planned across the country.

A 2025 state-ordered study found small modular reactors could be “a viable option for 24/7 carbon-free electricity in Indiana,” while offering more pay for workers than at coal plants. The Indiana Department of Energy Development also lauds potential economic impact from the reactors.

“Indiana’s retiring coal fleet represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to anchor next-generation energy, jobs, and tax base in communities that need it most,” the department states on the program’s website.

Participating communities can achieve three tiers requiring progressively more commitment. The earlier requirements are about educating the public about the form of energy, while later conditions include applications and more specific planning with utilities for nuclear development.

It’s those earlier commitments, about informing citizens about what nuclear could mean, that David Bottorff, executive director of the Association of Indiana Counties, thinks are especially valuable.

He said developers have previously announced large industrial projects before the public could even learn of or give feedback on them. That includes data centers, which have led nearly a third of Indiana counties to place moratoriums or other restrictions on their development until officials can learn more.

The Indiana Advanced Nuclear Ready Community program “is better coordination than trying to force the development in their community that is going to create pushback,” Bottorff said.

Kerwin Olson, executive director of Citizens Action Coalition, similarly sees the program as a way to get ahead of local backlash, much like that against data centers and wind and solar farm projects. But he said the push for nuclear power is out of a false belief that renewable energy sources can’t provide all the state’s electricity needs.

“It’s resistance to real clean energy — renewable energy — and hanging onto that sort of romantic relationship we have with big projects and base-load power plants,” Olson said.

He thinks nuclear development projects will only drive up costs for consumers, pointing to small modular reactor construction still being far off and how past nuclear work has floundered in development or come in over budget.

Olson said the latest state program is a continuation of “lots of PR, lots of propaganda, lots of talking points,” by the nuclear energy industry, “but little in the way of delivering actual results.”

text:
My new favorite unnecessary thing accomplished by the Oregon Legislature was passing the Climate Resilience Investment Act in 2025.

It was both unnecessary and good at the same time.

The Climate Resilience Investment Act requires the Oregon Investment Council and the state treasurer to take action to ensure they manage risks from climate change to state investments. The state controls billions of dollars in investments, including the money invested to pay for the state retirement plan, PERS.

“I could make an argument that this bill was not necessary.”

You know who said that?

Oregon State Treasurer Elizabeth Steiner. Steiner was the bill’s champion.

The bill didn’t go that far.

The Climate Resilience Investment Act was not a divestment bill. It didn’t require the state to get its investments out of fossil fuels or away from carbon.

Fundamentally, it didn’t require the state to change its focus from prioritizing risks and rewards when choosing investments. The goal for state investments is still: Get good returns. Investment in oil, gas and coal may no longer be as welcome as they once were. It does not mean the state would never hold such investments. The decision would have to be a sound one financially.

The bill also required an annual report to the Legislature. The report is the bill’s benefit.

The report is supposed to measure the carbon intensity of the state’s investments. The report issued earlier this year does show a decline in Oregon investments in fossil fuels and more toward clean energy.

The report says that: Emissions intensity in the Oregon Public Employees Retirement Fund dropped by more than 50%; climate-positive investments within the Real Assets portfolio increased from $1.2 billion as of January 1, 2022 to $2.4 billion as of June 30, 2025; Although fossil fuel holdings in Private Market funds increased from January 1, 2022, into 2023, that marked the peak for such investments and was the last time there was a year-over-year increase.

Since January 1, 2023 fossil fuel holdings have steadily declined.

Go deeper into the report and there are also warnings: “Many countries are retreating from net zero ambition and are not public with the data.” There are gaps in data and data reporting is not standardized. In other words, it can be difficult to pin down what is going on in some state investments.

The bottom line conclusion, though, is positive for people who want less carbon-intense Oregon investment. That direction is not because of the Climate Resilience Act. It is because of the direction of the market. Fossil fuels are not done and finished. The business case for green energy or companies taking action to avoid climate risk often makes them the smart investments. And that was before the war in Iran disrupted global oil prices.

“This work has not been without controversy,” Steiner wrote in the report. “Some feel we have gone too far, too fast. Others feel we have not gone far enough.”

The bill did not go that far. The market was already going.

Richard Coe is editorial page editor at The Bulletin and can be reached at richard.coe@bendbulletin.com.

text:
The automotive industry has long been known for razor-thin margins, but that narrative is slowly changing as more subscription services and advanced software technology flood into vehicles. In fact, General Motors' (GM +2.44%) OnStar subscription services ended the second quarter with deferred revenue of $6.3 billion -- an almost 50% year-over-year increase. Those subscription sales come with far higher margins than its traditional automotive business, giving investors a new angle on an age-old industry and its potential.

Let's dig in and see how GM's digital strategy, as well as rival Ford Motor Company's (F +1.55%), could change the game for their investors.

What's going on?

Rather than pushing sales of its OnStar and Super Cruise services to consumers at the point of purchase, General Motors is going about it in a different way. The automaker is bundling long-term prepaid OnStar and Super Cruise trials into new vehicle purchase prices. All 2025 and newer models include eight years of OnStar Basics, and select equipped models include three years of hands-free Super Cruise and associated connected services.

The idea behind this strategy is simple: General Motors is essentially casting the widest possible net it can over consumers, hoping that in three or eight years' time, those consumers will have become so accustomed to having those services that they will opt to purchase them outright in their next vehicle or transition to paid monthly or yearly digital plans to keep those features in the existing vehicle.

So far, the results are encouraging, with General Motors reporting that retention rates were roughly 30% to 40% of drivers continuing to pay for Super Cruise after the three-year prepaid term.

If you're wondering what deferred revenue (that $6.3 billion) is, it's this: By bundling these multiyear trials into the upfront purchase of the vehicles, in accounting terms, this is revenue that General Motors has already collected during the vehicle purchase. But because a portion of the revenue is derived from OnStar services delivered each month throughout the trial, the automaker can't claim it as earned revenue until that time comes.

Make no mistake, deferred revenue isn't some imaginary pile of cash General Motors won't get a chance to utilize. Rather, think of it as a massive financial backlog that gives transparency to highly profitable upcoming revenue.

Where GM goes from here

At the end of Q2, General Motors had $6.3 billion in deferred revenue and said it remains on pace to reach $7.5 billion in deferred revenue by the end of this year. Recognized revenue was $800 million during Q2, a 20% bump from the prior year, and it is on pace to recognize $3 billion through 2026. The rule of thumb is that these digital services like OnStar and Super Cruise check in with software-like gross profit margins, or roughly 70%. As an entire company, General Motors' gross profit margin fluctuated between 15% and 20% between 2020 and 2025.

General Motors is far from driving alone on this new path forward. Crosstown rival Ford Motor Company is doing something very similar with its BlueCruise -- also noted to deliver gross margins around 70%. Ford's BlueCruise subscription has an annual $495 price tag, or $49.99 monthly, and while it hasn't copied its rivals' upfront purchase strategy, it experienced an 88% rise in total hands-free miles driven globally last year and topped the half-billion, hands-free miles-driven threshold.

The major difference between the Detroit rivals is their strategies. As General Motors continues to cast its wide net, OnStar is expecting to add another 1 million subscribers in 2026 to reach nearly 13 million by year's end. Ford is experiencing rapid growth as demand increases, but without such a wide net as its rival, Ford brought its global total to 1.22 million vehicles with BlueCruise last year. At the end of 2025, it boasted an 80% increase in vehicles equipped from the prior year.

text:
BYD Co. Ltd. (ISIN CNE100000296) has become a central player in Chinas electric vehicle and battery industry, and BYD stock now reflects a combination of rapid volume growth, improving profitability, and an expanding international footprint in passenger cars and energy storage solutions. In its latest reported full year, BYD generated multi billion revenue and reported material growth in net profit compared with the prior year, underlining how operating leverage in electric vehicles and batteries is increasingly visible in the companys financials. For many retail investors, the interplay between unit growth, margins, and capital expenditures is now a primary lens through which they evaluate BYD stock.

Revenue and profit expansion

Over recent years, BYD has reported sustained growth in revenue, supported by rising deliveries of battery electric vehicles and plug in hybrid models as well as continued sales of buses, commercial vehicles, and rechargeable batteries. In its most recently available full year, BYD disclosed that consolidated revenue had risen markedly compared with the preceding year, with management highlighting higher volumes, improved product mix in passenger cars, and increased contributions from energy storage systems. The company also reported that net profit for the same period grew at a faster rate than revenue, indicating that operating efficiency gains and scale effects are beginning to flow through to the bottom line.

Viewed over a multiyear horizon, BYDs revenue trajectory underscores how the company has moved from being primarily a domestic Chinese automaker and battery supplier to a global participant in the electric mobility ecosystem. Revenue from automotive and related products now accounts for a substantial share of the company total, and the growth rate in this segment in the latest full year was meaningfully higher than the growth rate of its more mature businesses. This diversification within the automotive segment by drivetrain type and price band helps the company manage cyclical risks and competitive pressures from both domestic peers and international manufacturers.

Profitability metrics, such as operating margin and net margin, have also showed gradual improvement as BYD has expanded its higher value product offerings and optimized manufacturing processes. In the latest full year, operating income increased noticeably compared with the prior year and net margin widened, reflecting both cost discipline and a shift toward more profitable vehicle models and battery products. For investors, these profitability trends are particularly important, because they suggest that the company can fund substantial research, development, and capacity investments while still improving shareholder returns over time.

Vehicle deliveries and market share

BYDs rise in the electric vehicle market is closely tied to the sharp increase in annual vehicle deliveries, especially in battery electric cars and plug in hybrid models. In the most recently reported full year, BYD disclosed that total new energy vehicle deliveries reached a significantly higher level than in the prior year, with growth driven by strong demand in China and expanding exports to markets in Asia, Europe, and other regions. This increase in deliveries translated into a higher share of the Chinese new energy vehicle segment and contributed to more visibility for BYD stock among international investors tracking the global EV race.

Segment data from recent reporting periods shows that BYDs sales of battery electric vehicles increased at a robust pace, while its plug in hybrid models also captured consumers interest due to their blend of electric efficiency and flexible range. The company detailed that unit volumes in both segments rose compared with the previous year, and that average selling prices benefited from a richer product mix including mid range and premium offerings. This combination of volume growth and pricing support has a direct bearing on revenue and margin dynamics, reinforcing the fundamental case for BYD stock.

Beyond passenger cars, BYDs position in electric buses and commercial vehicles remains an important contributor to its overall delivery numbers. The company has supplied electric buses to multiple cities worldwide, and although this segment can be more cyclical due to public procurement cycles, it provides diversification and supports the companys reputation as a full spectrum electric mobility provider. Taken together, the delivery figures across passenger and commercial vehicles underscore how BYD has leveraged its battery technology and manufacturing scale to build a broad portfolio that can compete across several market niches simultaneously.

Battery and energy storage expansion

BYDs core competence in rechargeable batteries underpins both its automotive and non automotive businesses. The company reports that capacity in power batteries and energy storage batteries has expanded over recent years, enabling it to support growing electric vehicle volumes and provide solutions for grid scale and commercial energy storage projects. In the latest full year, revenue from batteries and related products increased compared with the prior year, reflecting higher volumes and broader adoption of BYDs battery technology in applications beyond cars.

The companys energy storage systems, deployed in residential, commercial, and utility scale projects, are increasingly relevant for investors because they diversify BYDs earnings base and tap into a structural trend toward renewable energy integration and grid stability. Earnings trends and guidance signals

For investors analyzing BYD stock, the pattern of earnings growth and the companys cautious but constructive guidance language are central components of the investment case. The reported year on year increases in revenue, net profit, and earnings per share suggest that BYDs strategy of combining high volume production with continual product upgrades is delivering financial results. At the same time, the emphasis on monitoring costs and competition indicates that management is aware of the risks inherent in a fast growing but intensely competitive industry.

Balance sheet, cash flow, and investment capacity

BYDs balance sheet and cash flow statements in recent reports reveal how the company funds its growth and manages financial risk. The latest annual report shows that total assets and equity have increased compared with the prior year, reflecting retained earnings and new investments in production capacity and technology development. The company also reports a mix of short term and long term borrowings, which it uses alongside operating cash flow to finance capital expenditures and working capital requirements.

Operating cash flow in the most recent full year was positive and grew compared with the previous year, driven by higher profitability and efficient working capital management. This cash generation supports BYDs ability to invest in new factories, research and development, and international expansion without relying solely on external financing. The companys financial disclosures also describe capital expenditures directed to key projects, including expansions of battery manufacturing capacity, vehicle assembly plants, and research centers focused on new energy technologies.

For BYD stock, the balance between investment and financial stability is critical. Investors often scrutinize leverage ratios, cash balances, and capital expenditure levels to assess whether the company can sustain its growth trajectory while maintaining resilience against economic or industry specific shocks. BYDs latest figures indicate that while it is committing substantial capital to expansion, it continues to generate sufficient earnings and operating cash flow to support these investments, suggesting a controlled approach to growth that may appeal to long term shareholders.

International expansion and regulatory environment

BYDs international strategy has become more visible over recent years as the company has begun exporting electric vehicles to multiple markets and has expanded its presence with localized operations and partnerships. Sales data for recent periods show that exports of passenger cars have increased from a low base, contributing to overall vehicle deliveries and diversifying geographic revenue sources. In several countries, BYD has launched specific models tailored to local consumer preferences, which helps the company compete against established international manufacturers.

The regulatory environment for electric vehicles and energy storage is a key factor in BYDs expansion. Government policies in China and abroad, including subsidies, tax incentives, and emissions regulations, influence demand for BYDs products and shape the competitive landscape. Recent policy updates in major markets have continued to encourage electrification, though some subsidies have been adjusted or phased out, requiring companies like BYD to rely more on intrinsic product competitiveness and cost efficiency.

BYDs reports acknowledge the importance of regulatory and policy risk, noting that changes in subsidies or environmental standards could affect demand or require product adjustments. However, the company also emphasizes its efforts to comply with safety, environmental, and quality standards in all markets where it operates, which is essential for maintaining its reputation and avoiding regulatory disruptions. For investors tracking BYD stock, understanding how the company navigates these regulatory dynamics is crucial for evaluating its ability to sustain international growth.

Competitive landscape and technology positioning

The competitive environment in electric vehicles and batteries is intense, with numerous domestic and international firms vying for market share. BYDs position in this landscape is anchored by its integrated technology stack, including proprietary battery chemistries, electric drivetrains, and vehicle platforms. In recent years, the company has introduced new generations of battery technology and vehicle architectures that improve energy density, safety, and cost efficiency, aligning its product portfolio with the evolving demands of consumers and regulatory requirements.

Competitors in China and global automakers are investing heavily in similar technologies, which means that BYD must continually innovate to maintain its edge. The companys research and development expenditure figures in recent reports show substantial investment in technology, with R&D spending rising compared with the prior year as BYD pursues advancements in batteries, electric powertrains, autonomous driving features, and connected car services. These investments are intended to support both near term product launches and long term technological leadership.

For BYD stock, the technology dimension is often central to investor discussions. The perceived strength of BYDs battery technology, its ability to achieve cost targets, and its progress in software and vehicle intelligence are all factors that influence valuation multiples. The companys reported R&D expenditures and descriptions of its technology roadmap provide tangible signals of its commitment to innovation, which can be weighed against competitive developments and industry benchmarks when assessing the companys strategic position.

Risk factors and resilience

BYD detailed a variety of risk factors in its most recent annual report and other disclosures, including macroeconomic risk, competitive pressure, regulatory changes, supply chain disruptions, and technological shifts. The company highlighted that demand for electric vehicles and batteries can be sensitive to economic conditions, consumer confidence, and government policies, and that intensified competition could lead to pricing pressure or higher marketing and research costs.

Supply chain risks, particularly in raw materials for batteries such as lithium, nickel, and other components, are another important consideration. BYDs vertical integration strategy helps mitigate some of these risks, but it also exposes the company to fluctuations in commodity prices and potential disruptions. The companys disclosures note steps taken to secure supply and manage procurement, including long term contracts and diversification of suppliers, which are meant to strengthen resilience.

Technological risk is also a factor, as rapid advancements in battery chemistry, charging technology, and vehicle software can alter competitive dynamics. BYD addresses this through continuous investment in R&D and partnerships, aiming to remain at the forefront of key developments. For investors evaluating BYD stock, these risk factors must be balanced against the companys strengths in scale, integration, and brand recognition in electric mobility and energy storage.

Representative product focus

Among BYDs many electric vehicle lines, one of the most visible representative products is its pure electric passenger car range, which showcases the companys battery technology, design capabilities, and software features. These models form a core part of BYDs new energy vehicle portfolio and contribute substantially to the revenue growth and unit volume increases observed in recent reporting periods. The success of these vehicles in both domestic and export markets demonstrates how BYDs combination of range, efficiency, and pricing can attract a broad customer base.

BYD stock and market context

BYD stock, traded primarily in Hong Kong through its listed shares as well as in other forms in additional markets, reflects the companys rapid expansion and its positioning in the global electric mobility and battery industry. Recent market data shows that the shares are trading near the upper end of their multiyear range, indicating that investors have priced in substantial growth expectations. The valuation is supported by the reported increases in revenue, net profit, vehicle deliveries, and battery sales, as well as by the companys continued investments in technology and international expansion. For retail investors, the key questions around BYD stock often revolve around the sustainability of this growth, the competitive environment, and the extent to which future earnings can justify current market capitalization levels.

title: The Solution to the Power Grid's Woes Might Just Be Sitting in Your Driveway | WIRED
description:

With EVs sitting idle all across a city, that adds up to some serious power.
The overall idea is for EVs to send power back to the grid when demand is highest, like when people return home from work and switch on appliances.
All told, V2G promises to turn consumers of electricity into more active participants in the grid, with power flowing both ways.
text:
You can’t tell when you’re passing one on the highway, but an electric vehicle may well have a superpower. It charges by plugging into the electric grid, of course, but it might also be able to send energy back into it. For a growing number of EVs, this vehicle-to-grid technology, or V2G, creates a revenue stream for drivers, who utilities pay to tap into their batteries when demand on the grid spikes.

Utilities across the country are pursuing pilot projects for the tech, figuring out how to coordinate hundreds, thousands, and eventually millions of EVs. To that end, today a coalition of companies—Eversource, National Grid, EnergyHub, Sunrun, and the Mobility House—is launching an early test of the technology in Massachusetts so utility customers can give it a try. Lessons learned here and elsewhere could drive the technique into the mainstream, making the grid more reliable and electricity cheaper, even if you don’t own an EV. “It’s great to have Massachusetts stepping into the lead here and doing this because these learnings are what’s going to allow this technology to scale,” said Chip Silverman, director of grid services at Sunrun, a solar and battery company.

In the new system, participants hook into an existing program called ConnectedSolutions, which allows homes to run off their residential batteries, among other things. Then when there’s a “demand response” event, like during a heat wave, EV batteries can help the grid keep up. Participants are compensated for this, just like some homeowners who provide energy from their solar panels.

“It’s really kind of a small number of hours per year that you’re discharging the battery,” said Russell Vare, vice president of vehicle-grid integration at the Mobility House North America, a provider of charging infrastructure. “It’s not necessarily like a daily discharge. It’s just during those peak times the events are called.”

Utilities like V2G because they’re dealing with escalating, overlapping challenges. For one, the demand for electricity is growing as more power-hungry data centers come online and people switch from internal combustion cars to EVs and from gas furnaces to heat pumps. At the same time, utilities are trying to ditch gas and coal in favor of renewables like wind and solar. These clean technologies, though, are intermittent, in that the wind isn’t always blowing and the sun isn’t always shining. Utilities need ways to bank energy for later use, which is why they’re building storage facilities and even using the Earth itself as a giant battery.

Already, Americans are struggling with skyrocketing energy prices for a variety of reasons. Utility shareholders are reaping profits, for instance, and customers are footing the bill for improvements, like burying power lines so they don’t spark wildfires or come down in a storm. Building battery facilities and stringing transmission lines will add still more costs—the inevitable price to pay for a cleaner, more reliable grid.

Except some of that spending may indeed be avoidable: The promise of V2G is that it can make electricity cheaper. While participants need a bidirectional charger to send energy back to the grid, a utility doesn’t need to reinvent the system as a whole. EV batteries are an existing, widespread, and reliable source of backup energy to tap into in times of high demand, like during the summer when everyone is running their air conditioning. “It’s the cheapest cost of flexible energy storage that will be available for the grid,” Vare said.

The hotter the planet gets, the more enticing V2G looks for utilities. People need additional AC to stay healthy, but the appliances require lots of power to run. If that energy isn’t coming from renewables, it’s causing even more warming and increasing demand for AC, and on and on. In a V2G system, vehicles that follow predictable schedules, like school buses and municipal fleets, will be especially useful, in addition to their batteries being enormous stores of energy. Even a typical EV battery, though, has around six times the capacity as a backup unit mounted outside a house.

While not all EVs have the hardware needed to tap into V2G, more models are, like the Nissan Leaf, coming equipped to do so. And as with any technology, bidirectional chargers will get cheaper over time. “As hardware costs come down, installation becomes simpler, and standards continue to mature, we expect vehicle-to-grid to become dramatically more accessible over the next several years,” said Seth Frader-Thompson, president of EnergyHub, in a statement.

With EVs sitting idle all across a city, that adds up to some serious power. So much so, in fact, that only a fraction of owners would need to participate for a program to adequately support the grid. But the more people who opt in, the better, as that gives a utility a broader base to draw from. “If you have a higher number of batteries out there in a virtual power plant, you can actually use less energy from each individual battery,” Silverman said. “But collectively, when you patch them all together and aggregate them, it comes out to a very large resource. And that’s really where the magic is.”

These early projects are figuring out how best to coordinate this, like with apps that let people specify when they typically use their vehicle to, say, get to work. (Participants in the new Massachusetts program are able to do this.) The overall idea is for EVs to send power back to the grid when demand is highest, like when people return home from work and switch on appliances. Then, as the night goes on, the vehicles can charge. This would be paired with another technique, known as active managed charging, which staggers when EVs juice up through the evening and early morning hours—that is, they’re not all doing so at 10 pm, which would suddenly and dramatically increase demand on the grid.

All told, V2G promises to turn consumers of electricity into more active participants in the grid, with power flowing both ways. Far from straining the grid to the point of collapse, EVs will instead help save it.
